#8867. Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:

That hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

As a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

That’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.)

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:

Is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

But the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

You’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!)

Grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a new skill.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

You can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

If you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Becky, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, is someone I immediately thought of when I read that initial email. She’s 77, and didn’t start going to the gym until she was 57. Here’s what she had to say:

I couldn’t have said it any better myself, Becky. 😊

No matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪

Whenever you’re ready, here are more ways we can help

1) Here’s an article with a bunch of different bodyweight exercises and progressions you can do at home.

2) Our coaches build programs specific to you and your needs. Here’s the exact system we use.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Best tri suits of 2026 rated and reviewed based on 10 criteria. (Photo: Triathlete)

When you look good, you feel good – and when you feel good, you race great. It’s no surprise, then, that when triathletes gear up for race day, they spend hours looking online for the best tri suit.

Indeed, in our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, 88% of respondents said aesthetics were at least “somewhat” important, with 38% saying they wouldn’t wear what they felt was an “ugly” kit.

But a great triathlon suit is more than good-looking – ideally, it also needs to fit well, carry your nutrition stash, provide an aero- and hydro-dynamic advantage, and protect the tender bits from chafing.

We’re asking a lot of tri suits these days, but the industry has stepped up to the challenge. Legacy brands like Zoot and Coeur, as well as newcomers Ryzon and Tri-Fit, have made it possible for triathletes to find not only a suit that meets their practical race-day needs but also shows off their own personal style.

With so many options available, we asked the Philly Tri Club and Triathlete contributors to help with real-world testing of the top triathlon suits of 2026. The 150-strong club is all about creating an inclusive training community, and club members in a variety of shapes and sizes put tri suits through the paces, wearing them through workouts and races and making note of what works and what doesn’t in their triathlon kit reviews. Here’s what they had to say about the best triathlon suits of 2026.

In our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, we asked readers what brands of triathlon apparel they had in their closets. Though more than 20 brands were represented, the top six are familiar names in the industry.

Pockets: 2 back pockets, 2 svelte front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

The Regna Elite Trisuit offers a custom fit via an app that completes an AI-powered body scan for a fit based on your unique features. For the ultimate test, we tasked Triathlete contributor Jon Dorn and his wife Heather with testing it out. Jon stands at 6’6” and is self-described as very slender. His wife is 5’3” “buxom, and more powerfully built,” according to Jon.

“I’ve finally found a tri suit that doesn’t chafe my ass or distract me as various sensitive parts start smarting,” said Jon.

Heather noted that the suit was a 95% perfect fit, though the midsection was slightly loose. As someone who doesn’t fit into the “one-size-fits-most” size structure, she was still quite pleased. “This is the best my undercarriage has felt in a tri kit in years,” she reported after a four-hour training ride.

Ultimately, the pair found that the price tag is the biggest deterrent and only really justifiable if you’re someone who doesn’t fit into a standard tri kit well.

If you’re looking for a budget triathlon suit for a sprint or Olympic triathlon that won’t chafe, the 2XU Core Tri Suit is a safe bet. It lacks adequate padding and pockets sizable enough to carry enough nutrition for long-course training or racing, but at the $200 price point, it’s a rare find for short-course racing.

It’s light on compression if that’s your preference and when it comes to breathability, the suit was disappointing, so ideally plan to wear it in more forgiving weather, as our tester found that it trapped heat and sweat more than other comparable suits.

Our tester found it hard to criticize anything about this suit because it fit snugly and comfortably. While she doesn’t normally wear sleeved tri suits, she was pleasantly surprised by how thin and breathable the fabric on these sleeves was, to the point that she forgot the sleeves were even there.

The tri suit has ample compression, especially in the core. The one detractor is that this suit only comes in black or black and white, which is a little generic and not as fun as some of the other options on this list. User beware, too: our tester noticed a bit of color leaking when handwashing the suit. Consider wearing the suit for shorter training sessions or wearing a belt with additional fuel, as the two back pockets are medium-sized and diagonally aligned.

Pockets: 3 back pockets, 2 inner front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

When it comes to tri suits, it’s the little details that make a brand stand out. In this case, Tri-Fit’s attention to pockets – six in total, including one explicitly for holding ice on your neck during hot races – is reason enough to consider the Vortex for a long-course race.

Testers liked the fit, fabric choice, design, pockets, and overall feel, noting that it looks great with small logos, lightweight fabric, and comfortable chamois padding for shorter events. The chest zips up tightly, preventing wind trap, and performed well during rides and runs.

However, there was substantial drag in the water, and the vent holes under the arms caused chafing – vented fabric would be preferable, as would slightly more compression on the legs. In all, however, the Tri Fit feels premium, and with a few minor design tweaks, could quickly become a favorite tri suit.

Pockets: 1 lower-back channel pocket, 1 neck ice pocket

This tri suit performed adequately in the heat, thanks to the use of smart temp technology, which dials up evaporation from the skin to the air as body temperature rises. The super-thin and light chamois also mitigates heat well, especially on long rides, and strategically-placed airflow channels on the shoulders and back help things feel cool and fast on the bike.

However, the top zipper rubbed against the chest, causing discomfort during running and biking. It also chafed at the neckline due to the lack of a zipper cover. Testers liked that it fit well, but disliked that the zipper needed a fabric cover and that the white top was see-through, especially when wet coming out of the swim or sweating on the run (women testers noted their sports bra was visible while wearing the suit in a race).

At $125, Black Bibs brand has created a budget-friendly triathlon suit that stands out in a market full of offerings $300 or more. But “budget” should not be conflated with “cheap” here – the suit fits well, provides exceptional compression, and is a classic style (men’s and women’s one-piece colorways include a solid black as well as a black bottom half with navy, burgundy, or white uppers). Openings for the legs and arms use silicone “power bands” to keep the suit secure throughout a workout or race, and no chafing was reported. The suit also proved extremely durable both on and off the race course, holding up through dozens of laundry cycles without shrinking, pilling, or splitting seams.

The initial impression of the chamois was mediocre, but improved with subsequent use and resolved itself after several rides. Testers reported drag when swimming, with the neckline sagging, and recommended use with a wetsuit. Dislikes included poor moisture wicking, especially in the upper body, and unusually high rear pockets.

Unlike some tri brands, where women’s suits are simply a smaller version of the men’s, Coeur tri suits are designed with a woman’s physique in mind, from the contours of the suit to the women’s specific seamless chamois. Testers also liked the supple fabric and one-piece design with a full front zipper and high-rise short beneath, allowing for breathability and extra roominess in the torso.

This tri suit performed exceptionally well on the swim and run, but some chafing was experienced on the bike – chamois cream is recommended. The arm openings run slightly small, so athletes with muscular arms should size up or opt for the sleeveless version. Luckily, Coeur offers a variety of competitively-priced women’s tri suit configurations in matching colorways: sleeved, sleeveless, sports bra/shorts, aero tops, and tri tops with built-in bras.

Testers liked the sleek, minimalist, and professional appearance of the monochromatic Arise tri suit, as well as its stretchy, comfortable, and “slippery” feel that allowed for movement and flexibility without chafing. It remained comfortable even when wet, ran true to size, didn’t create unnecessary drag, and worked well with other clothing. This tri suit generally performed well across all conditions and disciplines, with no reported poor performance or chafing.

However, a dime-sized hole appeared in the left armpit after two wears, which was surprising and disappointing, given the suit’s $335 price tag. Testers also wished the back pocket was deeper and had multiple compartments.

Pockets: 1 rear pocket, two side pockets, 3 interior pockets

Zoot has been a mainstay of triathlon apparel for more than 40 years, and for good reason – users recognize the balance of form and function present in many of its products. The suits, designed by endurance athletes, for endurance athletes, come in a variety of designs, including flashy patterns and colorways.

The latest offering from Zoot, the Ultra Tri P1, performed well during swims in the ocean, bike rides on a trainer and outside, and runs outside. Testers liked its comfortable and true-to-size fit as well as built-in UPF 35 sun protection fabric.

However, the pockets were not very big, making it difficult to carry proper nutrition during training rides or runs – testers recommended wearing the suit for short-course racing or long-course events only if nutrition on the course is plentiful. The zipper was also annoying and rubbed a bit, requiring multiple adjustments while running.

Overall, however, the suit was rated as “top-notch” for comfort, breathability, and weight.

Looking for more tri suit reviews? Check out our reviews of tri suits from Varlo, Swiss Side, Wyn, Synergy, and more in The Best Tri Suits for 2024.

#8865. How to Start a Workout When You Really Don’t Feel Like It (The Bridge Task Method)

If you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself. It’s the gear shift from “couch” to “go.”

A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.

Below is the 5-step version one of our coaching clients uses with her own students, plus a free worksheet to map your own.

A few weeks ago I was talking with Tabitha, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, about a challenge a lot of people face. ​ Some quick context: Tabitha is an executive function coach. She helps neurodivergent students and their families build the skills and systems that support their academic and personal goals. ​ And she noticed something: ​ The challenge of getting started on a workout is almost identical to the challenge her students face when trying to start homework. ​ This might sound familiar. You get home after a long day, mentally fried, and all you want to do is veg out on the couch. ​ In that state, getting up to cook a healthy dinner or go do a workout can feel really freaking hard.

Switching from a “YEAH!” task (chilling on the couch) to a “NAH!” task (workout/homework), is often harder than the task itself.

If we can make that gear shift less dramatic, it can make a big difference!

Instead of going from YEAH! to NAH!, you insert at least one task that’s just…MEH.

If you’re struggling to start your workout, don’t fight the gear change. Bridge it.

Add a little MEH to the mix and see what happens.

Tabitha put together a free worksheet that walks you through mapping your own task initiation sequence. Your personal YEAH -> MEH -> NAH.

Try it this week, and keep me posted on how it goes. ​ You got this. ​ -Matt

Whenever you’re ready, here are other ways we can help:

1) Not sure where to start? Take our Getting Started Quiz.

2) Want a coach who builds a plan and walks with you each step of the way? Learn about NF Coaching.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Humans featured are exceptional examples and do not guarantee individual success. Your experience and results may vary.

#8864. Biological age tests: Should you get one?

Johnson, the subject of the Netflix documentary Don’t Die, says he’s on a quest to achieve the lowest possible “biological age” (also known as bio age).

He reportedly spends millions each year on anti-aging treatments—dozens of daily supplements, weekly acid peels for his skin, injections to boost collagen production, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and plasma infusions extracted from his 17-year-old son’s body.

To determine what’s working, Johnson has undergone numerous tests to assess his bio age. Johnson says these tests show his age is now 5.1 years younger than when he embarked on his anti-aging quest.

Granted, not everyone’s buying it. A New York Times exposé, for example, claims Johnson’s biological age, in reality, has increased by 10 years.1

Still, Johnson’s “don’t die” crusade is gaining traction.

Bio age tests are a frequent topic on popular podcasts by Peter Attia, Joe Rogan, and Andrew Huberman. Google “bio age testing” and you’ll see dozens of ads for mail-order blood or urine testing kits that claim to reveal your biological age, pace of aging, and more. With prices tumbling into affordability, it’s natural to wonder…

Should you or your client sign up for bio age testing?

If so, which test is best? Just as importantly, what should you do with the information?

Your biological age (bio age) refers to how your cells function. It’s not necessarily the same as your chronological age, which refers to the number of candles on your birthday cake.

For example, let’s say Chang, a 50-year-old man, works at a desk, spends his free time in front of the TV, lives in the most polluted city in the world, eats a candy bar for lunch, and smokes. On the other hand, Jabari, a different 50-year-old man, hits the gym several times a week, lives in the mountains, doesn’t smoke, relishes his five servings of veggies a day, meditates, and spends most evenings in his garden.

Genetics aside, you’d be wise to wager that Jabari’s bio age is younger than Chang’s.

Bio age testing kits measure one or more biological markers of aging, also known as biomarkers.

For example, some tests focus on the size of your telomeres, the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes. Others measure DNA methylation, a physiological process that chemically alters DNA.

Once a company isolates and measures these markers from your blood or urine, it plugs the bio data into a formula that calculates your bio age.

However, if you see a doctor with any regularity, you’re likely already tracking some biomarkers of aging. For example, biomarkers such as blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and blood glucose can help predict your risk of future cardiovascular disease, a leading cause of premature death.

Biomarker testing can help you monitor your wellness proactively rather than waiting for disease symptoms to appear.

For some, it also serves as a motivator. If you learn you have the bones of someone 20 years older, this may give you the nudge you need to start strength training consistently.

In addition, biomarkers provide objective data, allowing you to track and evaluate various health-related actions quantitatively. By monitoring your blood pressure, you might learn that consistent exercise helps, but your late-afternoon energy drink does the opposite.

You don’t have to be a billionaire (or even a millionaire) to track biomarkers of aging.

In this section, we’ll cover several massively underappreciated, scientifically validated tests you can use to gain insight into your bio age—for FREE.

Before scientists developed high-tech blood-based bio age tests, researchers used these free tests to calculate the pace of aging in the people they studied.

People who are fitter and stronger tend to live longer.2

That’s because muscles do more than just move us around. They also secrete anti-inflammatory substances, help to regulate blood sugar, slow cellular aging, protect the lining of the arteries, and more. All this helps reduce the risk of age-related diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease, a phenomenon we explore in our article, The New Science of Muscle.

Related to strength, your ability to balance is also key. If you’re middle-aged or older and can’t stand on one foot for at least 10 seconds, your risk of dying in the next seven years is double that of someone who can stand for longer, according to a study of 1,700 people.3

The Sitting-Rising Test (SRT) is one way to assess both strength and balance at the same time.

People with low scores on this test have a higher risk of dying from cardiovascular disease, according to a 12-year study of 4,200 adults between the ages of 46 and 75.4

Lower yourself to the floor with your legs in a crisscross position. Then, with your legs in the same position, stand back up. As you stand, notice if you must use a part of your body—hand, shin, knee—as leverage.

To score yourself, start with 10 points. Then, for each body part you used to stand, deduct a point. Subtract a half point if you became unsteady or lost your balance.

Keep in mind that this (and other tests) serve as a proxy for your fitness. A low score indicates that your balance and coordination, muscle strength and power, and mobility may all require some attention.

Like the SRT test, your grip strength provides insight into your overall fitness. If the muscles in your hands are weak, the muscles throughout your body are more likely to be weak, too.

Poor grip strength can also predict future muscle weakness. In one study, people with a weak grip were more likely to walk slowly and be unable to rise from a chair, complete rigorous housework, or climb a flight of steps 25 years later.5

Low grip strength has also been associated with:6

According to one study, grip strength was a better indicator of longevity (or lack thereof) than blood pressure.7

Grab a standard tennis ball, and squeeze as hard as you can, for as long as you can.

If you can manage 15 to 30 seconds before your grip fatigues, you’re doing fine. Ninety seconds puts you well above average—anything over 90 ranks you solidly in the upper-third percentile.

If you’re below 15, keep in mind that this test is also just one indicator of your overall strength. (And squeezing balls to improve grip strength without training the rest of your body is unlikely to make significant improvements in your overall health and fitness.)

A hand-held dynamometer—available for use at most occupational therapists’ and some gyms—can also test grip strength. (If you’re willing to shell out some cash, you can buy your own for somewhere between $100 and $500.)

An ability to balance on one foot for an extended period can help reduce your risk of falls, one of the leading causes of injury-related death among older adults.

In addition, many different bodily systems—the eyes, inner ear, skeletal muscles, and brain—must work together to help you stay upright.

Conditions like diabetes, heart disease, and cancer can all affect balance. As a result, an inability to stand on one foot can serve as a warning sign for eroding health and fitness.8

Stand near a wall or chair for safety. Keep your eyes open and hands on your hips. Then, lift your dominant leg and start timing yourself. Once you put your foot down, stop the clock. Repeat the test with your non-dominant leg.

Once you have your times, compare them to the following averages, from a study out of Duke University, to see how you did compared to your age-matched peers.9

Sometimes you know why you’re tired, such as the morning after binge-watching the last few episodes of a thriller. Once you catch up on your sleep, the weariness lifts.

That’s not the same thing as fatigue, which describes persistent exhaustion that worsens over time and interferes with life. In addition to feeling physically tired, someone who’s fatigued feels mentally dull and emotionally exhausted.

Think of fatigue as an early sign that something’s off, especially if you don’t know the cause.

Let’s say you’ve already ruled out the usual suspects like too much caffeine, dehydration, too much alcohol, medication side effects, chronic stress, or too much or too little exercise. What’s left is likely a sleep disorder or a developing health problem such as anemia, obesity, depression, cancer, or diabetes, to name a few.

If you’re 60 or older, fatiguability—or how worn out you feel after an activity—can also predict longevity.

According to research out of the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, the higher someone scores in fatiguability, the higher their risk of death in the future.10 Other research has linked high fatiguability with declines in gait speed, walking ability, and other tests of fitness.11

To measure fatigability, use a tool called the Pittsburgh Fatigability Scale. Using a 0 (no fatigue) to 5 (extreme fatigue) scale, rate how fatigued you think you would feel after completing the following activities:

If you score less than 15, you’re doing well. Scores between 15 and 24 are a warning sign. Anything 25 and above is regarded as severe, and worth mentioning to your healthcare professional.12

Despite popular belief, both too little and too much body fat can influence health for the worse, as we explore in our infographic, Is body fat good or bad for you?

Your muscle mass also plays a role, which is why someone’s body composition matters more than their weight.

The gold standard methods that estimate body composition—underwater weighing, air displacement (Bod Pod), and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA)—certainly aren’t free.

However, a recent study determined that a good old-fashioned (and cheap) tape measure can provide a comparably accurate estimate of body composition.13

To use a tape measure to keep track of your body fat percentage, measure:

Ensure the tape is snug but not so tight that it cuts into the skin. Once you have your measurements, plug those numbers—along with your age, sex, height, and weight—into our FREE Body Fat Calculator, which will take it from there.

Depending on where you live in the world, the following tests may not be free. However, as part of routine preventative care, your insurance might cover them.

If your primary care doctor recommends yearly blood work, it’s for good reason.

By keeping tabs on several blood markers, you can see if your health is trending toward type 2 diabetes or heart disease, both leading causes of premature mortality.

Many blood markers can also be influenced relatively quickly (within 6 to 12 weeks) through lifestyle changes, supplement protocols, or medications. This makes them practical tools for monitoring whether various lifestyle or medical modifications are working.

If you’re not already doing so, consider having the following blood markers tested annually. Then, talk to your health care professional about what your numbers mean. They might use the following numbers, along with your blood pressure, to calculate a cardiovascular disease risk score.

*Milligrams per deciliter of blood **Milligrams per liter

When researchers study healthy super-agers aged 90 and older, strong bones are one of their defining features.14

That may be because, like muscles, bones are live organs that secrete substances that may be beneficial to overall health and longevity.15

For example, bones secrete osteocalcin, a hormone that plays a role in bone remodeling. When osteocalcin circulates in the body, it’s thought to play a role in everything from helping muscles to produce ATP to regulating brain neurotransmitters.

Because of these varied roles, it’s thought that, as bones wear away, osteocalcin levels drop, contributing to many age-related health problems, including diabetes, low muscle mass, and cognitive issues.16 17 (At least, that’s the theory. Most of this research has been done on mice.)

Osteocalcin aside, loss of bone density can, of course, lead to fractures, which can increase your risk of death for up to 10 years after a break.18

It’s especially important to keep tabs on bone health if you’re in any of these high-risk categories:

Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans are a type of X-ray that measures the amount of bone mineral content packed into a square centimeter of bone.

Insurance often won’t cover these scans for people younger than 65 unless there’s a documented risk of developing osteoporosis. Out of pocket, the average cost is about $300.

When you receive your DEXA results, you’ll see a T-score that represents how your bone density compares to the average bone density of a young adult with peak bone mass. A T-score of +1.0 to -1.0 means you have normal bone mineral density for someone your age. Anything below -1.0 means you might have osteopenia (low bone mineral density) or osteoporosis (porous bones that are prone to fracture).

If you have some money to burn, you can learn an awful lot about your body.

Here, you’ll find a quick run-down on some of the more high-tech tests you can get and what they can tell you.

However, before we get into the details, we want to point out a few caveats:

▶ Biological age can vary over time, and by organ. Someone may go through a period of accelerated aging—saying, during a period of intense stress—then their rate of aging may slow as they focus more on recovery. Additionally, organs can age at different rates. For example, someone with heart disease may have a relatively older heart than their kidneys. (Not all tests measure individual organ age, but it’s becoming more common.)

▶ Commercial tests won’t always accurately reflect the changes you’re making. Until more research supports the reliability of these tests, evaluate your behaviors over isolated test results. If you’re eating more fruits and veggies, exercising more consistently, managing stress, and otherwise slaying the healthy lifestyle department, don’t sweat your results. Focus on doing the things we know improve health.

▶ If a company pairs your test results with a hard sell for a proprietary and expensive supplement protocol, be wary. It’s better to share and discuss your results with a trusted health professional than take health advice from a profit-seeking stranger over the internet.

DNA methylation is a biological process that chemically alters DNA. Because the rate of methylation accelerates with aging, it can be used to estimate someone’s biological age and life expectancy, finds research.19 20 21

The Horvath Clock and DunedinPACE both measure specific biomarkers that can be used to better understand someone’s methylation rate. Scientists developed these tests to help other scientists study how various lifestyle factors, environmental exposures, and medicines affect aging. They didn’t develop the tests as a way for the average person to pinpoint their biological age. (Which hasn’t stopped companies from selling DNA methylation testing kits to the public.) They cost about $300.

If you decide to get one of these tests, keep in mind your results won’t give you a complete picture of your health and longevity. Aging typically occurs at varying rates throughout the body. Your liver might age faster than your heart or brain, for example. So if you measure DNA methylation in your blood, that’s all you know about. Put another way, a DNA methylation test isn’t a substitute for your annual wellness checkup or blood work.

Telomeres—the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes—wear away with age. The length of a telomere can predict how many times a specific cell can divide before dying.

Abnormally short telomeres are associated with several genetic diseases. For this reason, when physicians suspect someone might have inherited a genetic disease, they’ll order a specific type of telomere test—the flow-FISH test—to measure the telomere length in all the cells in a blood sample.22 23

It’s more debatable whether telomere tests can predict aging in healthy people.

Just as importantly, the telomere test marketed to the public, known as the qPCR telomere test, isn’t used in research or medicine. These $100 tests are fine if you’re merely curious—just don’t base health and fitness decisions on your results.

For years, only elite athletes cared about VO2 max, which describes the maximum amount of oxygen that your body can use during exercise.

More recently, however, some experts have suggested that VO2 max can serve as a measure for athletes and non-athletes alike to track the rate at which their bodies are aging.

People with high VO2 max tend not only to be more physically fit but also less likely to develop heart disease, diabetes, cancer, or stroke.24 25 26 27

In an observational study that followed the health outcomes of 5,107 Danish men over 46 years, men with above-average V02 max during middle age lived an average of five years longer than men with below-average V02 max. Each unit increase in VO2 max was associated with a 45-day increase in longevity. The researchers suggested VO2 max may more accurately predict all-cause mortality than high cholesterol, obesity, high blood pressure, and insulin resistance.28

You might think of V02 max as a canary and your aging body as a coal mine.

As you age, your chest wall becomes more rigid, the muscles that surround the lungs weaker, and the oxygen-carrying blood vessels calcified and less elastic. The heart also squeezes with less force, max heart rate drops, muscle mass and strength decline, the mitochondria in cells and muscles lose their effectiveness, among other differences.

In addition to raising your risk for many different diseases, these changes can also affect VO2 max, which tends to decline 10 percent per decade starting around age 30.29 30

In the past, the only way to reliably measure VO2 max was in a fitness lab.

You would wear a metabolic mask and a heart monitor while you ran or cycled to exhaustion. The mask collected your expired carbon dioxide and monitored how much oxygen you sucked into your lungs. This lab-based testing is still the most accurate way to measure V02 max as well as other key fitness metrics such as:

Depending on where you live, you might be able to get your VO2 max tested for around $150.

However, if you don’t have access to a VO2 max clinic, three somewhat less accurate options exist.

Wear a heart rate monitor as you walk one mile on a flat surface, such as a treadmill or running track. As soon as you complete the mile, record your heart rate and walk time. Then, plug it into the following formula to calculate your VO2 max:

132.853 — (0.0769 × Weight) — (0.3877 × Age) + (6.315 × Sex) — (3.2649 × Time) — (0.1565 × Heart rate)

If that feels like too much math, you can also use a free online tool.

Many smartwatches will estimate your VO2 Max for you based on information the watch gathers from your workouts, sex, and age. Compared to in-office testing, smart watches can over- or underestimate V02 max, especially in people who are very out of shape or extremely fit.31

Because of this, you don’t necessarily want to use your smart watch measurement to determine your current state of health. However, it can help you to see trends. For example, does your VO2 estimate drop after a few weeks of skipping your usual spin class? If so, that’s good information to have.

Fitness performance correlates with longevity. If you’re getting faster at running a certain distance or can go a longer distance than before, you’re getting fitter and increasing your chances of living a long, healthy life.

One way to test this: the 12-minute run test, also known as the Cooper test. (This is a validated way to estimate VO2 max—and shows about a 90 percent correlation with lab-based measurements.)

Run as fast as you can on a flat surface, such as a treadmill set at a 1 percent incline or running track, for 12 minutes. After 12 minutes, record your distance. Then, plug it into one of the following formulas to calculate your VO2 max.

In lieu of doing math, you can also use a free online calculator.

Try to think of the information you gather about your body as just that—information.

It’s not a moral judgment of who you are as a person.

Just as importantly, it’s not a permanent situation.

You have options. However, most people make two big mistakes when it comes to longevity-related lifestyle changes.

It’s the simple, boring, “I’ve heard this a million times before” health practices that, when done consistently, add up to a long, healthy life.

According to thousands of studies, people who practice these and other high-impact strategies not only live longer, but also live better. They’re stronger, happier, and less likely to spend their later years disabled or in pain.

(If you’d like to see where you stand when it comes to big impact health and longevity strategies, check out our FREE Longevity Assessment.)

However, when it comes to health, fitness, and longevity, many people pursue options with minimal impact (at best). They reach for the latest, trendy supplement rather than taking steps to quit smoking, as just one example.

Here’s the thing: Big rock strategies require changes in behavior. If daily physical activity were as easy as popping a pill, walkers and cyclists would clog up the streets in your neighborhood.

(It’s precisely this reason why so many people need the support of a certified health coach who has undergone training in the science of behavior change.)

The data gathered from biomarker aging tests can give you a sense of control.

Data, in isolation, doesn’t lead to a longer life.

Gathering data without changing your behavior is like checking your reflection in the mirror, seeing spinach wedged between your incisors, and leaving it there.

You need to remove the spinach for the mirror check to be worthwhile.

If you don’t use your bio data to inform behavior change, you’re wasting your money and time.

Consider your biomarker data as a baseline or starting point.

Then, use it to assess whether various lifestyle changes or medical interventions are moving you closer to your goal of living a longer, healthier life.

#8863. I Took Marijuana Edibles to Find Out If Weed Makes You Faster—Or If It Just Feels That Way

The ride felt easier and more immersive—find out if the data told a different story.

I still remember my first time in Colorado after weed was legalized. I walked into a dispensary and my mind was blown by the very chill and knowledgeable manager at the shop walking me through all the strains available. He pointed out the anticipated vibes around each one and which were the best options for activities like rides and trail runs.

Marijuana use in outdoor sports is not new, but efforts to study its effect on performance have been gaining steam. Everyone from the University of Colorado Boulder to the Gatorade Sports Science Institute is putting resources into how this substance impacts endurance sports.

More states have legalized recreational marijuana and many cyclists I’ve talked to have asked whether there are performance benefits or risks. While there are several helpful studies on the effects of marijuana on endurance athletes, none focus on cycling.

With few specific answers available, I wanted to put together my own test. Since I live in New Jersey, a state where recreational weed is legal, I bought a pack of edibles from a local dispensary and gathered all of the sensors I have available. Then I put together a simple study. In the safety of my own home, I would jump on Zwift, following the same route before and after taking edibles. The location was important. While research on marijuana’s impact on cycling performance is rare, multiple studies have shown that THC can impair coordination and slow reaction times, two factors that can increase the risk of cycling, especially outside the relatively controlled environment of my home trainer setup.

To keep outside variables in check, I rode the trainer through Zwift’s Loopin Lava route. I chose this route because I wanted something less than 60 minutes (including warmup and cooldown) that had sustained climbing sections as well as some flat and rolling sections to get a bit of variety. In all, it has about 690 feet of climbing over 11.5 miles.

I aimed to average about 185 watts (roughly zone two) on both tests—keeping my power output the same on both rides, I hoped, would reveal something about weed’s effects on my workout.

My home lab felt like it was made for this moment. As a health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and longtime fitness industry professional, I’ve been growing my collection of sensors for years—I was using a Garmin heart-rate sensor, a power meter built into the Wahoo trainer, a CORE temperature sensor, a Nix sweat sensor, and I used a pulse oximeter to check my oxygen saturation levels in 10-minute intervals. These sensors gave me insight into things I was curious about for the test—I even used my Coros Pace 4 as a backup. Does heart rate change? How does sweat rate and sweat content change after some gummies? Does internal body temperature or oxygen saturation rise or fall after a little weed? I was about to find out.

I did my baseline ride first, then took about a 90-minute break to let my internal temperature reset and let my body reset. Once I finished my first ride I took 40 milligrams of marijuana edibles and gave them some time to kick in (yes, that’s a relatively large dose; I wanted to make sure I experienced the full effects of the edibles on my riding in this not-too-scientific test).

I pulled all the data through Strava, the CORE app, the Nix app, and then pooled it into two columns of an Excel spreadsheet. This was the easiest way to get all the data into one place for analysis.

I opted for edibles after reading several peer-reviewed articles that found that smoking in general can cause changes in heart rate. Edibles would remove that variable, as well as make it easy to consume a target dose. With edibles the math was simple—4 gummies contained 40 milligrams. I had some idea what I was getting into. A 2023 study in the journal Sports Medicine, looked at the effects of marijuana on runners jogging on a treadmill.

One of its findings was that weed could help athletes get a jump on tapping into the runner’s high. “It is possible that exogenous cannabinoids like THC or CBD might activate the endocannabinoid system in a way that mimics the runner’s high,” said Laurel Gibson, PhD, a researcher on the project. It was time for me to find out.

I wasn't "in Barstow on the edge of the desert when the drugs began to kick in," as Hunter S. Thompson wrote in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas—I was in my basement getting ready to get back on the trainer. I queued up a chill electronic playlist to tap into the beats with my pedal stroke. I did the same 15-minute warmup I did prior to the first ride while I got all my sensors dialed in. Toward the end of my warmup I noticed something—I was getting sucked into the ride. If you’ve ever been on a trainer ride, then you know that the monotony of riding indoors can make you want to hit the eject button as soon as possible. On my first ride I was watching the clock to see when I’d be done, but on this warmup I quickly felt myself getting more hooked on my cadence.

Once the test ride started, I felt like I was more immersed in the virtual world compared to the baseline ride—I was the avatar. As I spun up and down hills, I focused on my breathing and cadence. I felt locked in, in a way that couldn’t have been more different from the first ride. I just wanted to keep going.

Even though it felt harder to push the same watts on this ride, I didn’t want to stop once the route was done. I had to remind myself that I was doing this as an experiment and it was time to get off the bike—I could have kept pedaling around that virtual world for hours. Again—not surprising. The Sports Medicine study found that marijuana increases enjoyment, enhances recovery, and heightens motivation during workouts. In these ways, at least, it seems marijuana’s effects on cyclists are similar to the runners in the study.

It turns out weed is not a performance-enhancing drug for me. Comparing the two rides showed there was a noticeable difference in heart rate as well as body temperature—two traditional indicators of performance. During the roughly 32-minute effort, my average heart rate went up 28 beats per minute (bpm) while my max internal body temperature went up almost a full degree after taking the 40mg dose. That suggests the THC and CBD in the gummies had a negative effect on my performance. While I wasn’t too surprised by this, I was surprised by what I felt versus what the numbers showed.

For an expert opinion, I shared my results with Angela D. Bryan, PhD, adjunct professor, Division of Medical Oncology at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, editor in chief of Annals of Behavioral Medicine, and a researcher on the 2023 Sports Medicine study. She quickly zeroed in on my 40mg dose and the rise in heart rate. “That’s a huge dose, actually, and THC itself causes an acute increase in heart rate. So that’s why you saw that,” she said. Her note on heart rate is important because if THC raises heart rate, that in and of itself can impact performance.

I didn’t have a drop in my ability to sustain power, and I didn’t notice an inability to recover when I tried to put in a dig on the climb. The biggest performance takeaway I had is this: THC and CBD can raise heart rate while riding, which can impact performance. But oddly, in the moment I didn’t feel that I was working harder or that my heart was pounding faster. This is a different and potentially positive effect of marijuana.

Not everyone is training for high performance—a lot of us just want to ride more. During my edible test I didn’t dread getting on the trainer, and once I was on it, I didn’t want to get off. I might have had a higher heart rate, but I enjoyed the experience significantly more. I could see this fitting in on trainer rides in general and zone one, recovery, or zone two rides more specifically. Of course, more research needs to be done on the long-term effects of THC and CBD on athletes.

This was just one trial, at a relatively high dosage. Overall, I found the experience pleasant, and the impact on performance modest—and the idea of experiencing the “runner’s high” sooner is appealing—especially on trainer rides.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8862. Does Soreness Mean a Good Workout? No. Here’s What It Actually Tells You

Soreness is not an indicator of a good workout, and not being sore doesn’t mean your workout didn’t count.

That day-after ache (DOMS) mostly tells you that you did something new, not something effective.

Progress is more reliably measured in your training log: more weight, more reps, more control over time, sore or not.

Rachael (a reader and all-around amazing person) sent me a question about this so well-organized it came with multiple choice answers. 😃

I LOVE this question, because almost everyone who’s getting started (or starting again) wonders the same thing:

Quick definition first. That achy, stiff, “why does it hurt to sit on the toilet” feeling that shows up a day or two after a workout has a name: DOMS, or Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness.

It usually peaks somewhere around 24-72 hours after you train.

Severe soreness is NOT an indicator of a good workout.

It’s a sign that you did something new that your body isn’t used to yet:

But it’s also not something to be afraid of, especially if you switch up your routine and are mildly sore for a day or two.

Your body is adapting quickly! And as you adjust to the new exercises, you’ll be less and less sore from it.

So when is soreness helpful, if ever? ​ Soreness can give us a useful signal that we worked a muscle we were trying to target and hadn’t felt before.

But if you’re SUPER sore? Like, can’t get out of bed the next day and have to waddle around like a newborn giraffe sore? That’s a sign the jump was bigger than your body needed.

And the real cost (beyond the discomfort) is that it gets in the way of your next couple of workouts. Either because your technique gets sloppy because everything hurts, or you’re so wrecked that you don’t want to show up at all.

The best way to lower your odds of severe DOMS is to ease into a new program slowly.

Start with fewer sets and lighter weights than you think you need, and build from there. 💪

Yes! You DO need to push yourself over time in order to make progress:

That’s the law of progressive overload, and there’s no getting around it.

Sometimes adding that extra bit will make you sore. Other times, it won’t.

But it’s the underlying principle that matters: are you asking a little more of yourself over time? Not: did it hurt afterward?

So why do we care so much about soreness?

Here’s what I think we’ve fallen into with fitness in general.

We as humans operate really well with feedback. If we touch a hot stove, we get burned and know not to do that again.

We want to know, immediately after doing something, whether it worked or it didn’t.

And with strength training, you don’t feel stronger the next day. It takes time to build up.

So we reach for proxies that close that feedback loop.

It’s exactly like the story of minty toothpaste.

As the story goes, toothpaste manufacturers had a hard time selling their product until they added mint.

Suddenly, there was a tingly clean feeling you could latch onto. “Oh, this IS working.”

The mint doesn’t clean your teeth. But it’s associated with the thing that does, and it gave people something to feel.

It’s not the REASON you’re getting stronger.

But it can be associated with the work you do, especially as a beginner who is new to exercise, so we’ve learned to chase the tingle.

✅ How much weight, how many reps, how many sets are you doing?

✅ Do you feel more stable and controlled with the exercise than you did last month?

Then great! It’s working. Doesn’t matter if you never get sore.

And if you do end up super sore after trying something new, it’s not that you “failed”.

Just take it as a cue to introduce things more gently next time. 😊

So, back to Rachael’s multiple choice question.

C is really close. But I’ll add an fourth option:

D) Soreness tells you what was NEW. Your training log tells you what’s WORKING.

No extra fitness points for being sore. No points off if you do end up sore, either.

All the points gently ramping things up over time, and showing up again next time. 🔥

Is it bad if I’m never sore? No. If your weights, reps, or control are improving over time, your training is working, sore or not.

How long does DOMS last? It usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after the workout and fades over a few days. If you’re regularly wrecked for longer, ease the jumps in your program.

Should I work out while sore? Mild soreness is fine to train through, and easy movement often helps. If you’re severely sore, target a different part of the body, scale down, or take another rest day; what we don’t want to do is have sloppy technique because we’re SO sore we can’t perform the exercise normally.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

#8861. Can Your Road Bike Handle a Cyclocross Race?

A 33mm tire may fit, but mud clearance, gearing, and frame durability still matter.

A decade ago, it was still common to see Tour pros racing on 23mm tires, with 25mm considered progressive. Views on tire width have shifted. At this year’s Tour de France, most riders were on tires labeled 28mm to 30mm; mounted and inflated, many measured 30mm to 32.5mm. The widest setups measured in the paddock were more than 33mm—above the UCI cyclocross limit.

Road bikes with room for 32mm tires are increasingly common. Some clear rubber as wide as 40mm. So you might be wondering: Can I install a pair of 33mm cyclocross tires on my road bike and race the local ’cross?

As these photos show, I mounted 33mm cyclocross tires on Trek’s Madone 8 road bike. And there was even a bit of clearance, even though Trek states the Madone’s maximum tire clearance is 32mm.

But just because you can doesn’t mean you should. There’s more to racing cyclocross on a road bike than stuffing knobbies into any frame that clears them.

CX race bikes are designed to take a 33mm knobby tire with generous mud clearance. A road bike’s stated maximum tire width leaves room for some debris around a slick tread, but not for peanut-butter mud.

Then there is all the other stuff you will find on a cyclocross course: sand, ruts, off-camber turns, barriers, and sharp corners.

You’ll dismount, shoulder the bike, pound into bumps and holes, and crash.

Your road frame wasn’t built with all of cyclocross’s many charms in mind. The engineers I’ve asked about this point to the seatstays as particularly vulnerable to damage in cyclocross.

There is precedent, though. Toon Aerts won the 2025 European Cyclocross Championships on an Orbea Orca OMX road frame fitted with a fork from the Orbea Terra Race gravel bike. That’s a pro-level workaround for a sponsored athlete, not a green light for every road bike.

Your road bike’s gearing is probably too high for a ‘cross course, which is likely to feature steep, slippery climbs and slow technical sections. Road gearing can mean more dismounts; an easier gear can help keep you riding instead of getting off to push.

If you want to race ‘cross without buying a cyclocross bike, a gravel bike is a better place to start. It usually has lower gearing and is built for bigger impacts and rougher use. A gravel bike definitely has room for a 33mm tire. If it’s a modern model built for 50mm-plus tires, it’ll have heaps of mud clearance—so much that a 33mm CX tire might look a little lost in there.

And if you use your gravel bike, you can also use wider gravel tires. The UCI caps CX tire width at 33mm, but that only applies to races they sanction.

Your local CX series is probably not UCI-sanctioned.

Local rules vary, so check before you line up. If wider tires are allowed, a wider gravel tire may offer more comfort and grip—and could even be faster, depending on the course.

There’s a handling trade-off. CX bikes are made to whip through tight, slower-speed corners; gravel bikes usually favor stability. So a gravel bike might feel too long, too stable, and the steering too slow, on a tight ‘cross course. But you might actually prefer a more placid-handling gravel bike in the anaerobic blur of a cyclocross race.

So, can you ‘cross your road bike? Technically, yes—if a 33mm tire clears without rubbing, the course is dry, and your gearing suits the terrain. But just because you can doesn’t mean you should. If you already have a gravel bike, start there. Check the rules, fit the tires, and go have a race.

#8860. How Fast Do You Actually Lose Strength? Slower Than You Think

You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.

A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).

Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.

Here’s the timeline, and how it can inform your training.

Has this question ever crossed your mind:

This was an awesome question that Charles sent my way. (Thanks Charles! 🙌)

When life gets crazy and you find yourself skipping workouts, there’s a voice that says:

I had that exact thought the first time I had to take significant time away for a back injury.

And heck, just recently my kiddos brought home the “crud” from school and I missed a full week of workouts.

So, let’s look at what actually happens, and what it means for your training.

Short version: a few days off doesn’t impact your maximum strength or muscle size basically at all.

Your muscles may look or feel “flatter”, but that’s because stored water and glycogen decrease, not because you are weaker.

And this “pump” comes back quickly once you start training again. 💪

Here’s a rough timeline of when we start to see the effects of detraining:

Highly trained folks and older adults will notice detraining faster than new or younger lifters (so they’ll sit towards the beginning of these timelines.)

But you don’t lose your progress in any meaningful way after a week or 2 away from the gym. 😊

And if you DO have to spend significant time away for whatever reason, I have good news for you, too:

1) Your nervous system remembers how to do the movement.

The first session or two in the gym after time away may feel a bit clunky, but you’ll quickly regain the technique.

And a big component of strength is neuromuscular coordination (i.e. your brain and muscles firing together more efficiently, which improves rapidly.)

2) The muscle itself seems to hold onto some of the machinery it built, so it rebuilds faster the second time.

A general rule of thumb is about 50% as long as you were away (so if you were away for 12 weeks, it may take ~6 weeks to rebuild your strength.) Take this with a grain of salt as there is a LOT of variation here. This isn’t a hard and fast rule.

(And you don’t want to jump right back in at 100%. Use the 50/50 rule to get yourself going again.)

The point is, it’s generally easier to rebuild than to build the first time.

Building muscle and strength? It takes time and effort.

No one wakes up a day after a workout and has just magically put on 5 pounds of muscle.

That takes only a fraction of the volume.

When you keep intensity the same (i.e. how hard the exercise is), doing 1/3 the number of sets maintains your strength for a loooong time. ​ The point being: doing ANYTHING during a period where you aren’t able to consistently work out is still really really helpful!

When life throws you off track with your fitness goals, you’re not starting back from square zero.

And even a single session each week with a couple challenging sets is enough to hold what you’ve built until things calm down.

There’s that old saying that: “The best time to invest was 20 years ago. The next best time to invest is today.”

I think the same holds true for building up your fitness.

Every session you put in now is strength you get to keep later.

This is exactly why we built our coaching program. Because having a coach makes both of those so much smoother. ​ We take the thinking off your plate so it’s easier to get going.

We direct your limited time and effort toward the stuff that actually moves the needle. ​ AND when life pulls you away (sick kids, a work deadline, etc.) we help you maintain and get right back at it. ​ If that sounds like the kind of help you’ve been looking for, here’s how NF Coaching works. 💪 ​ -Matt

#8859. These Are the Three Accessories You Need for a New Bike—And the One You Don’t

The right accessories can make your first rides safer, smoother, and more fun.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

During my time working in bike shops, I have sold hundreds, if not over a thousand, bikes, and significantly more accessories. I’ve seen some people buy every accessory under the sun while they get their new bike, and others opt out of any accessories other than a bottle cage. A bottle cage is a good start, but there are a few other accessories to make sure you have the best possible first ride.

New bike day is a big day. The price of a new bike from a name brand manufacturer can be a big expense, so it’s understandable to hesitate when having to buy more. However, I’ve seen too many bikes become a clothes rack in a basement because someone didn’t have the experience they were hoping for on those first crucial rides. Getting the right gear from day one can change those initial impressions from negative to positive, but be aware you don’t need to buy all the things at once.

Here we’ll talk about the three accessories I recommend on day one, the one accessory I’ve steered a lot of riders away from when getting a new bike, and a few honorable mentions to consider as you ride more. Whether you’re a seasoned rider or just looking for tips on your first bike purchase, this story is for you.

Assuming you’re buying a bike that comes with pedals, helmets have always been the first piece of gear I suggest to riders buying a new bike. While helmets are not foolproof, they are a significant line of defense in keeping you safe as a rider. I’ve personally broken five helmets over the years, one of those times the doctor told me it likely saved my life. Keep in mind you don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars on a great helmet. When considering a new helmet, Virginia Tech Helmet Rating is the go-to resource on helmet safety testing.

Tara Seplavy, deputy editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on some of the Bicycling team’s favorite picks from the top-rated Virginia Tech helmets. One of the highest value helmets from the top ten on the Virginia Tech list is the P2R A20 Mips. This helmet comes in at only $60. “With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price,” says Seplavy.

If you’re buying your fifth bike and think you don’t need a new helmet, consider this—most of the major helmet manufacturers recommend replacing a helmet every three to five years. This is due to things like sun exposure, normal use, and even repetitive small impacts over time. For riders looking for a higher level of performance out of a budget helmet, then consider the aero helmet from P2R. It’s priced at $100 and as our resident tester Tom Messina said, “it has no business being this good.”

I know, I know—a flat kit consists of multiple accessories. Typically my basic flat kit for people getting a new bike consists of: some type of inflation, tire levers, a multitool, the correct tube for the new bike, and something to carry it in. Some brands sell a flat pack that consists of all the above. If your new bike has internal storage and you plan on putting your flat kit in there, just be sure to make sure it all fits before your first ride.

Even for riders that have multiple bikes I suggest a new flat kit. Bikes have different requirements for tube sizes and valve types and lengths for different rims. There’s nothing worse than getting a flat and taking everything apart just to realize you have the wrong size tube or your valve isn’t long enough (let alone if your spare tube has a Schrader valve, but you need a presta).

If you have multiple bikes keeping a flat kit on each one also makes sense because when you’re taking a bike out you don’t have to switch around the flat kit. This means you’re less likely to forget something, and it takes away a hurdle from you getting out the door.

There are plenty of options to go with when considering inflation. I typically carry one to two CO2 cartridges and a CO2 inflator in a flat pack or frame storage because they take up such little room and can (sometimes) reset a bead on a tubeless tire. I also carry a frame-mounted hand pump on longer rides, because I’ve been stranded after running out of CO2 in the past. Mini electric inflators have been gaining steam in the past few years, and the convenience of them is hard to pass up.

A lot of bikes these days have more than one place to put a bottle cage, so if your new bike allows I suggest going with two bottle cages. Current full-suspension mountain bikes typically only fit one (I’m not a fan of a bottle on the down tube of a mountain bike), so that’s an exception to the suggestion.

I typically suggest recommending bottle cages to people getting a new bike over something like a hydration pack. The most impactful reason is because when you use a hydration pack it puts more weight on your sit bones when you ride. Water is one of the heaviest things you’ll carry on the bike, but you need it as you ride. Since you have to bring it, put that weight on the bike instead of having the weight sit on your sit bones.

There are two honorable mentions worth talking about—one has to do with safety and the other has to do with comfort. The first is a taillight. I didn’t mention it above because it’s less of a necessity if you’re strictly trail riding off road.

One of the things I would always hear about in the shop was, “but I’m not riding at night so I don’t need a tail light.” Daytime running lights have that name for a reason—you run them day or night. These lights help increase visibility of cyclists as we share the road with vehicles. Drivers can more easily spot riders thanks to varying strobe patterns of the light and some even have radar and cameras built in like the Garmin Varia series of lights. The radar in the Varia detects cars coming from behind and gives you a heads up on your phone, watch, or head unit. I couldn’t imagine riding on the road without a radar taillight at this point.

The second honorable mention is a pair of cycling shorts—specifically bike shorts that have a built-in chamois pad. These shorts help improve comfort like few other things when riding a bike. It took me years to convince my wife to try them, but now she won’t ride without a pair. I’ve tried a lot of bike shorts and I’ve learned that the bib style stay in place better throughout a ride compared to the standard shorts.

Another essential piece of advice when picking the right chamois is you get what you pay for. I’ve tried a $20 Amazon pair and I’m currently testing the Dottore Clima Bib Shorts from Q36.5. The Q36.5 bibs are by far the most comfortable bike shorts I have ever tried whether I’m doing shorter lunch rides or doing 100 mile gravel days. The flip side is they are also by far the most expensive pair of bike shorts I’ve ever tried, but there is a significant level of comfort no matter how many hours I’m in the saddle.

At this point it is safe to say that many of us have a smartphone. There are always exceptions, but throughout my time working in a shop I’ve come across a small handful of folks still using a flip phone. In addition to smartphones becoming an ingrained part of society, smartwatches are seen more and more on people’s wrists. If you have either of those things you don’t need a bike computer—especially to get into riding.

Bike computers are nice to have for training purposes and navigating a new area or route. But most of those things can be done on a phone or smart watch these days. I have used watches from Apple, COROS, and Garmin for tracking rides, navigation, and as a guide for training on a ride with success. If you’re a new rider and have a smartphone I typically suggest downloading Strava because it’s easy to track rides, the navigation tool is fairly user-friendly, and it’s easy to see your progress the more you ride.

Don’t get me wrong—I love my bike computer. It pools data from my heart-rate sensor, CORE body temperature sensor, cadence and power from my power meters, and even my sweat data through my Nix sensor. I can see every metric I can think of and most head units allow you to customize the layout on the screen. But the reality is that a worthwhile head unit is typically a few hundred dollars. Conversely the phone mount that I typically suggest costs less than $30 and is fairly universal. Bike computers make sense for some riders, but don’t start here if you’re prioritizing certain accessories over others for your new bike.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8858. Why You Keep Falling Off Your Fitness Routine (and the 2-Minute Plan That Fixes It)

Expecting yourself to stick to the same fitness routine, no matter what, is why it fails.

Because the only predictable thing about life is that it’s unpredictable.

A kid gets sick. Sleep falls apart. The to-do list explodes.

You can’t know which one is coming or when, but you can know something is, and you can build your routine to expect it.

That’s the whole trick: take two minutes and decide, in advance, exactly what you’ll do the next time life goes sideways.

Here’s the coaching conversation that shows how it works.

I want to let you in on one of my biggest lessons from the last 15 years of coaching.

Once you know it, it will feel like you can see the future. 👀

On a live Q&A, George (not his real name) told me about a pattern he kept running into.

Then a kiddo would get sick, or some other responsibility would pop up, sleep would fall apart for a bit, and the whole routine would go with it.

And he got this look like “Oooooohhhhhhhh…no. No I haven’t.”

He’d been treating the sick kid as something that happens to the plan.

So we talked through it right there. Here’s what we came up with:

Now, he wasn’t just reacting in the moment, trying to “gut it out.”

He knew exactly what to do and it fit what he needed.

Here’s the thing: these moments don’t come out of the blue. They are predictable.

You’ll have WAY too much on your to-do list.

I don’t know which one, or when exactly, but I do know that it’s inevitable.

Once we accept that the only predictable thing is that life is unpredictable, we can use that to our advantage.

Take two minutes right now and finish this sentence:

First blank: the thing that knocked you off track the last time you were trying to get into a fitness routine.

Second blank: the best version of your plan you can still commit to on one of THOSE days.

Sometimes, life will throw something at you that you REALLY didn’t see coming.

But the more of these you’ve been through, the clearer the crystal ball becomes.

And the better you get at navigating it. 💪

Hit reply and send me your crystal ball plan. I read every one, and I’ll tell you if I’d tweak it.

-Matt ​ ​P.S. This is exactly the type of stuff we work on in our coaching program. My job as your coach is to look into my crystal ball, and help you plan ahead so you don’t get blindsided. 🔮👀 Learn more about how coaching works [HERE].
