#8822. Does Breathing Deeply Feel Hard? Yoga Can Help.

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about deep breathing first appeared in the March-April 2004 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

With each breath you take, a symphony of muscular activity occurs. As you inhale, some muscles contract while others relax. The result is an expanded space for the lungs, and thus for the breath. As you exhale, the space you need to breathe shrinks—again, through a complex set of muscular actions. For smooth and effective breathing to take place, the muscles involved in the breathing deeply must be fine-tuned and coordinated, just like the instruments of an orchestra.

The lungs don’t have the power to expand and contract on their own: They are inflated by air pressure to the size of their container, the rib cage. The rib cage in turn is expanded or compressed by the surrounding muscles. The breath orchestra includes many different muscles in the chest, back, neck, and abdomen, but none are as important as the diaphragm, which plays a primary role in expanding the breathing space during inhalation and helping control the shrinkage during exhalation.

You can visualize the diaphragm as half a basketball that attaches all the way around the lower ribs. When the diaphragm relaxes, it arches up toward the heart. When it contracts, it becomes flatter, pushing down toward the abdomen. Most of the sensation you feel when you inhale comes from the outward expansion of the belly and lower ribs, a movement created by the contraction of the diaphragm. This contraction lengthens the space available for the lungs and expands the rib cage to the front, the back, and the sides, causing air to be drawn into the lungs. When you exhale, the reverse happens: The diaphragm relaxes, arching up again; your belly becomes flatter; and the rib cage shrinks, pushing the air back out.

Anything that restricts the movement of the diaphragm restricts the breath, especially limiting the ability to inhale fully. There are many conditions that can constrict the diaphragm, including wearing overly tight clothes or a belt cinched too snugly around the waist. Another common cause is slumped posture. Sit up tall and notice how the lower ribs lift up off the abdomen and the adjacent upper belly becomes spacious. Now slump forward, letting your spine round back and your head jut forward. In this position, you’ll feel the lower ribs dig back and in toward the spine, compressing the diaphragm and the upper belly.

Retaining the space your diaphragm needs to move freely is only one of the many reasons it’s a good idea to work on your everyday posture; it’s also a good reason to be conscious of your spinal alignment in seated forward bends. If you work too aggressively to get your head toward the floor in these poses, your spine will round backward and your diaphragm will become compressed.

The movement of the diaphragm can also be restricted by tightness in the abdominal muscles. Pain or fear can lead to gripping in this area; combine that with holding your breath—another common habitual response to anxiety—and you have a recipe for an all-but-immobilized diaphragm. The abdominals can also become overly tight and short through too much focus on abdominal strengthening exercises like curl-ups and crunches.

Each time you curl your head and chest off the floor, you recreate a slumped position and train the abdominals to pull the lower ribs down toward the navel and back toward the spine. If the abs are never given a counterbalancing stretch, they will constantly hold the ribs in that constricted position.

Now don’t get me wrong. I absolutely believe that the ab muscles must be kept strong and conditioned. Their strength is important in supporting the abdominal organs and lower back. It’s also needed to compress the abdomen, assisting in exhalation, and for such forceful exhalations as coughing, sneezing, and fast breathing during exercise.

So the abdominal muscles need to be strong enough to perform their jobs, but they should not be so short, tight, and rigid that they restrict lung expansion and limit inhalation. The upper abdominals, which are strengthened during curl-ups and crunches, are the guilty gang that can put the squeeze on the diaphragm. These upper abdominals include the upper fibers of the rectus abdominus, which sits lengthwise in the center of the abdomen, running between the pubic bone below and the lower sternum and the rib cartilage above. The external and internal obliques, which cross the abdomen diagonally like a supporting girdle, also have upper fibers that attach to the lower ribs and can restrict rib cage movement.

To return to the musical analogy, rigid and short abdominals can overpower the rest of the breath orchestra and limit the contribution that other muscles—especially the diaphragm —can make to the symphony of the breath. Besides disturbing the proper balance between the different muscles involved in breathing deeply, and thus disturbing the breath’s rhythm, tight upper abdominals can contribute to chronic neck pain and headaches. When the expansion of the lower lung space is restricted, we tend to compensate by over-expanding the upper lung space. In this situation, the muscles that lift the rib cage and expand the space between the upper ribs—including the sternocleidomastoid muscles (on the front of the neck) and the upper trapezius muscles (on the back of the neck)—have to do much more than their usual share of the work during inhalation. Neck strain and chronic neck tension are often the result. And the most common cause of headaches is neck tension, especially the excessive pull on the base of the skull where the upper trapezius attaches.

To keep your obliques and rectus abdominus in optimal working order, you must train them to relax and lengthen as well as to contract and shorten. You can begin this process simply by taking a few moments after abdominal strengthening exercises or poses to invite the abs to relax.

Lying on your back, place your hands on your belly, with your fingers spreading out below your navel. When you inhale, your diaphragm will contract and push down on your belly, which will expand under your hands. This upward and outward expansion indicates that the abdominals have released and are lengthening

The abdominal muscles will lengthen even more if you recline over a bolster.

With your hips on the floor, lie back on the bolster so your torso and head are supported, your arms are relaxed out to the sides, and your chest is open. If you position the end of the bolster just at the bottom of your ribs, you’ll lengthen the upper abdominals and create space for the diaphragm. Now take a few minutes to breathe slowly and steadily, feeling the expansion of each inhalation as it gets drawn down into the lower rib cage and upper belly

Along with this exercise, many backbends can help stretch the abs, including Camel Pose (Ustrasana), Upward-Facing Bow Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana), and Bridge Pose (Setu Bandha Sarvangasana).

If your diaphragm has been limited for years by snug waistbands, tight ab muscles, slumped posture, or habitual breath-holding, it may be too out of condition to contribute much to the breathing process. You can strengthen the diaphragm by providing some resistance to its work. Lying on your back, place some weight on your belly.

The appropriate weight will vary according to your size and ability, from one to two pounds (perhaps a bag of rice) to eight to 10 pounds (a yoga sandbag) or even more. But it should always be something that is soft and can spread, so it will sit comfortably in place. As your belly expands each time you inhale, the diaphragm will have to work harder to lift the extra weight.

Breathe slowly for a few minutes, working for a smooth breath pattern.

With practice, you can create an appropriate balance in the muscles of your belly—a balance that allows them to relax as your diaphragm contracts during inhalation yet keeps them strong enough to support the lower back and assist in exhalation. As your awareness of the diaphragm increases, you may find yourself opting for looser clothes and for seated and standing positions that don’t compress your belly. You may also begin to notice when you respond to stress, anger, and other emotions by holding your breath and tightening your abdomen—and realize that your tension melts away when you release your grip, allowing your diaphragm to move and your breath to flow. After all, the smooth, beautiful music of the breath is not just an important focus in yoga and meditation; it can help you stay centered and calm even as the storms of life rage around you.

#8821. Wow! Jess McClain Becomes the First American Woman on the NYC Marathon Podium in 8 Years

McClain outsprinted reigning champion Hellen Obiri to finish as runner-up.

Jess McClain, the 34-year-old from Scottsdale, Arizona, who has been a fan favorite ever since she reemerged on the American running scene with her fourth-place finish at the Olympic Marathon Trials in 2024, finished second at the New York City Marathon in 2:24:42.

She said in an interview with ESPN after the race that she didn’t feel great through the first 18 miles. But it was a good day not to feel great, because the race went out in a pedestrian 1:13:52 for the first half.

As the lead pack made its way up Fifth Avenue, McClain’s face betrayed no pain. She also wasn’t alone—three other American women, Weini Kelati, the American record holder in the half marathon, making her debut, Carrie Ellwood, and Paige Wood—were also in the lead pack.

The race broke open at mile 23 with eventual champion Sheila Chepkirui and defending champion Hellen Obiri, both of Kenya, creating a seven-second gap.

But McClain, in her mint green Brooks kit, was always visible lurking in the distance.

And notably, she ran the tangents through the curves of Central Park, while the leaders stayed in the middle of the road, adding distance.

“The last two miles through the park, I was just like really focused on the tangents and my form,” McClain said. “And I was taking the shortest line possible, and I kind of noticed Hellen kind of not taking the tangents, and I think honestly, like, every small percentage of anything helped in the last few miles.”

McClain stayed within striking distance and ran 5:10 for the 25th mile. As they turned off of Central Park South and back into Central Park, they passed the sign that reads, “400 meters to go.”

Chepkirui opened up in the final 200 meters, winning by six seconds. And with mere feet to go until the finish line, McClain overtook Obiri.

McClain is no stranger to Central Park, having raced the women’s Mini 10K in June and the Dash to the Finish Line 5K the day before the New York City Marathon. She was eighth in the NYC Marathon in 2024.

“I just felt really strong with 400 to go,” she said. “I've been able to like visualize this last 200 to 400, and I just went straight to the arms last 200.”

She outsprinted Obiri, who has three Olympic medals, including two silver medals at the 5,000 meters.

Behind McClain, Ellwood, 32, finished sixth in 2:26:28, Kelati, 29, was seventh in 2:26:51, and Wood, 30, was eighth in 2:27:29, bold racing against tough international competition. Ellwood didn’t merit a bio page in the New York City Marathon media guide, although she ran 2:22:53 at Boston in April.

Combining prize money for top 10 overall and for top American finishes, McClain, who works full-time for nonprofits in Arizona, won $85,000. Ellwood earns $25,000, and Kelati takes home $17,500.

The last American woman to make the podium at New York was Shalane Flanagan, who was third in 2018 and won in 2017.

McClain’s top-five finish gives her qualification for the Olympic marathon in 2028; but first she’ll need to finish in the top three at the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials to make it to the Los Angeles Games.

McClain is about three years into her second go-around with professional running. She graduated from Stanford University in 2015 and turned pro with Brooks, joining the Brooks Beasts track club in Seattle. But her progress was slow and she was disappointed with her results.

She stepped away from the professional running world and moved back to her home state of Arizona during the pandemic and began training with local men, running a downhill marathon in 2022 and finishing fourth at Grandma’s Marathon in Minnesota in 2023, before that fourth-place finish at the Trials in 2024.

She’s been steady atop the ranks of American marathoning ever since. She was eighth at the World Championships in the marathon in 2025 and ran her PR of 2:20:49 at Boston in April. McClain’s also not afraid to stay in touch with her track roots and race 5Ks and 10Ks on the oval. In March this year, in the thick of marathon training for Boston, she put on her spikes and ran 31:15 for 10,000 meters.

This week, in the lead-up to the race, she had practiced running the final 400 meters a few times, getting reacquainted with New York’s uphill finish, and visualizing herself on it.

“I was like, no matter where I am in the race, I’m going to hammer it home,” she said. “It’s not over till it’s over.”

#8820. This $16 Tool Can Save You Thousands of Dollars Across the Life Span of Your Bike

Catch chain wear early and you could save hundreds—or more—on drivetrain replacements.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I’ve checked in thousands of bikes for service, and I used to hear this line all the time: “I ride the bike a lot, but it’s in great shape. The shifting just jumps around a little.” Once I would get to the step of putting a chain checker on the chain, that $16 tool might tell the story of hundreds of dollars in upcoming repairs.

A chain checker was one of my most recommended service tools to customers when I ran a bike shop service department. The key is to make sure you are buying the correct one and understand how to use it. The chain checker most shops I worked in was the Park Tool CC2 —the chain checker with the swivel dial.

This option was great because it gave customers and service advisors an easy visual on the wear level of a chain. But the biggest reason my favorite chain checker isn’t this one is because it does not give a clear reading on certain SRAM chains. Read on to find out which chain checker I suggest, why it can save you thousands of dollars across the life span of your bike, and how to use this small tool.

When a chain gets stretched it can cause issues like slow shifting, unexpected chain jumps, and the chain can have a slipping feeling under power. Sometimes these issues can also be mistaken for cable tension being off in a derailleur, but you can easily check the chain stretch at home if you have this chain checker.

It is extremely difficult to tell how worn a drivetrain is with the naked eye. By checking how worn a chain is, you can tell what other parts will need to be replaced. My favorite chain checker is the Pedro’s Chain Checker because it is compatible with most chain makes and models. It also retails for only $16 and it is small enough to fit in almost anyone’s tool roll or kit.

Many shops will recommend replacing an 11, 12, or 13 speed chain when a chain checker reads over 50 percent worn. If the chain is over 75 percent worn that recommendation changes to replacing a chain and cassette or freewheel (gears on the back wheel) and replacing chain, cassette or freewheel, and chainrings or crank (gears in the front near the pedals) when it measures over 100 percent worn. Typically 10-speed chains and lower have a bigger tolerance to stretch, with singlespeeds having the biggest acceptable stretch.

Many times a customer would ask if the shop could just throw a new chain onto a drivetrain that is past that 100 percent mark. If you do this, the shifting can actually get worse because the wear pattern in the new chain no longer lines up with the wear pattern on the existing cassette and chainrings. An even worse case scenario of putting a new chain on a worn drivetrain is chain suck. This is when a worn chainring can get stuck to the chain from the bottom of the pedal stroke. Then the chain gets sucked up and jammed between the chainring and the frame—possibly leading to damage on the frame. Once a drivetrain has a certain level of wear replacing only one part of the system does not work.

The price for some higher-end cassettes can range anywhere from $400 to $660 from brands like Shimano and SRAM. I go by a three-strike rule with chains (spokes too, but that’s a different story). For my own bikes I typically get three chains out of each cassette.

If you are on top of chain wear with a chain checker, this could save you almost $2,000 in cassette costs alone when using high-end SRAM cassettes. Remember, this price doesn’t include labor or the cost of chainrings—which you’ll need to replace if you keep running the chain until it’s above that 100 percent wear mark.

Some higher-end chainrings, like the SRAM Red direct-mount chainring, can run up to almost $300 per ring. If someone runs the whole drivetrain into the ground, then a checkup for shifting issues can quickly turn into a thousand-dollar bill on a high end drivetrain. If you’re running Shimano 105 or SRAM Rival, then being on top of chain wear might not save you thousands as quickly as running the highest end group set. Rest assured, overtime you’ll get there too. The better news is that Pedro's chain checker is so easy to use.

Start by dropping the tooth with the number one above it into the chain. Once the number one tooth is dropped in, then drop the tooth with the number two above it into the chain. Finally, try to drop the third tooth (numbered with a three) into the chain. If this tooth doesn’t drop in through the links in the chain, then good news! Your chain is less than 50 percent worn. If it drops halfway through the chain that means your chain is about 75 percent worn. Finally, if the tooth numbered three on the chain checker drops all the way through the chain that means it is between 75 percent and 100 percent worn. Typically I suggest if you have 11, 12, or 13 speed chains around that 50 percent worn mark change the chain soon to keep the rest drivetrain alive as long as possible.

#8819. Triathlon News, October 2026: Ironman Crashes, NYC Tri Returns, Middle East Racing

Tim Heming highlights the biggest news in triathlon in October 2026. (Photo: Triathlete)

In October, the triathlon world turned its eyes to the Big Island for another epic edition of the Ironman World Championship, but that didn’t stop the rest of the multisport world from serving up its usual mix of drama, debate, and headline-grabbing news.

From analyzing the sparse participation numbers at New York’s long-awaited race return to tackling safety, transparency, and course caps following a scary collision on the Queen K, October delivered plenty of food for thought. And, as always, contributor Tim Heming is here to digest it with you.

The first line of Sarah Wassner Flynn’s article about the return of the iconic New York City Triathlon, published earlier this year, reads: “For more than two decades, the New York City Triathlon was one of the sport’s most iconic races. Debuting in 2001, it quickly became a bucket-list event for age-groupers and pros alike.”

The piece previewed this year’s race return, renamed the Big Apple Triathlon, under new ownership of Alpha Win, formerly known as HITS Endurance, with Tommy Struzzieri taking over the company from his father, Tom.

Alpha Win, based in Saugerties, New York, is no novice when it comes to race hosting. They have put on over 200 races, but making a success of this one offered the sternest test of their credentials to date.

Held on October 10, the day when most eyes in the triathlon world were focused almost 5,000 miles west on the Big Island of Hawaii, would it prove enough of a draw to justify the set-up costs of a swim in the Hudson River, a bike up the closed West Side Highway, and a run through Central Park?

Since its halcyon days, the event has been beset by problems, with participation tumbling from a peak of almost 4,000 during its time as part of the Life Time Fitness Series in 2010. In 2024, it was canceled by new owner Supertri before registration even opened, with organizers saying they couldn’t find a suitable date. It didn’t return in 2025 either, which, given Supertri’s focus on producing stylish, short-course events in major urban areas, had to be a worrying sign.

“We’re just trying to bring back something that athletes have been asking for,” Struzzieri said in March, noting that numbers would be capped at 2,500. If that felt optimistic, a New York Post piece on the eve of the event recounted its troubled history and asked: Is this time the charm? stating that around 1,300 athletes were expected to start, with prices ranging from $350–$650.

The results, however, show fewer than half that number: only around 600 finishers across all formats, the lowest the event has seen since it began in 2001. “Every year that there’s an issue with this event, it hurts the event the following year,” Scott Nilson, Supertri’s U.S. general manager of events, told us in 2024. Perhaps this year it will be the simple economics of numbers.

Registration for the 2027 event is now open with early-bird pricing (including processing fees) at $548.90 (Olympic distance) and $383.90 (sprint distance). Triathlete reached out to Alpha Win for comment.

For the majority, the Ironman World Championship is a day of celebration and achievement. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience, the ultimate triathlon dream. For Trish Byron, that dream turned into a nightmare.

Byron was struck by a male cyclist from behind almost 30 miles into the bike leg, leaving her with seven fractured ribs, a broken collarbone, a punctured and partially collapsed lung, a concussion, a laceration requiring stitches, and extensive road rash.

It’s understood the cyclist stopped and spoke with volunteers before continuing the race, but Byron’s daughter Cassie Anne put out a plea on Facebook for more information, saying: “We’re hoping to gather firsthand accounts, identify the cyclist involved, and better understand what happened.”

Accidents happen, but the incident raises questions about transparency when serious collisions occur during races. Should such incidents be publicly reported, both to demonstrate that appropriate safety protocols and follow-up procedures have been followed and to help triathletes better understand the risks involved in signing up?

Cassie Anne’s post received a response from Judy Daggett, who said: “This exact scenario happened to me on the bike about mile 85, causing me to crash also. The guy who hit me kept going. Another athlete helped me to my feet.

“I immediately had double vision and said, ‘Yes, I need help,’ but there was no one around. I managed to get back on the bike and ride to T2, praying my vision didn’t completely leave.

“When I got there, they took me by ambulance to the ER for a CT of my head, thinking I could possibly have a brain bleed. Thankfully, I did not, but I also have fractured ribs, a hip and shoulder injury, and a concussion.”

Daggett went on to say she’d reached out to Ironman but was yet to hear from them, stating it was her first DNF in 30 years and that the “men were so aggressive, they need to let them go first”.

Her final point relates to the questions raised about the scheduled swim start waves that interspersed the men’s and women’s age-group divisions in Hawaii, whereas previously, the men had been started earlier in one cohort, followed by the women.

It also brings into focus the broader question (that has continued to surface since the announcement of the return to one day of racing) of whether Ironman should cap numbers on the course for both fairness and safety reasons.

While it might seem that Trish Byron’s family shouldn’t have far to go to find answers, as Anna Grosz, who also responded to the post, explained, it might not be that simple: “I provided medical support for the race. We are bound by patient confidentiality laws. You should reach out to Ironman through official channels. The medical director may be able to communicate directly with the affected athlete, but course volunteers cannot do so.”

Triathlete has contacted Ironman for comment.

Championship season is not quite over in the world of triathlon. The T100 Tour still has three events on the calendar, with Dubai and Saudi Arabia in November ahead of the T100 World Championship Final in Qatar. The action in the Middle East will also continue with the 2026 World Triathlon Multisport Championship in Abu Dhabi.

The headlines will be the professional races over 100K where Hayden Wilde looks to be the odds-on favorite to retain his title, and it’s wide open on the women’s side. But there is also shorter-distance racing and representative age-group competition throughout.

Despite conflict in the region and the cancelation, postponement or relocation of other major sporting events, particularly in Saudi Arabia, both World Triathlon and the Professional Triathletes Organization are, for now, proceeding as planned. That’s perhaps to be expected, with contingency decisions often left until the last possible moment. But if the events do go ahead, it will be interesting to see how much appetite international athletes have for traveling to the region.

Conversations around weight can be a sensitive topic: triggering to some, frustrating to others, and almost irrelevant to others. And Susan Kitchen’s article on why we shouldn’t be concerning ourselves with post-race weight gain will no doubt grab the attention of athletes who might have concerns about how they can be heavier after doing all that exercise.

While Kitchen spells out the reasons here (which, spoiler alert, can be perfectly natural as your body recovers), it also made me think that perhaps the concern shouldn’t be how much you weigh, but why, in the days following an incredible endurance feat, you’re not off celebrating somewhere, rather than hopping on the scale.

You may not find an answer as to which is better, but there is plenty we can learn from Jordan Blanco’s roundtable discussion with triathlon legends Flora Duffy and Jan Frodeno when it comes to their appreciation for the pinnacle events in our sport – including that the 2008 win in Beijing was Frodeno’s first-ever elite victory!

But if there is one takeaway, then it’s probably that following your heart is the first step, and the financial rewards will follow. Doing it the other way around might just be a little tougher.

What do we learn from the Kona bike mechanics recounting tales from the Big Island?

Number one: That most of us should probably invest a bit more time in understanding how to fix our own bikes.

Number two: That whatever daft mistake you’ve made, it won’t be the dumbest thing they’ve seen (one athlete rolled up with two front wheels and no back, another with two back wheels and no front).

Number three: If you do have a problem, get to the mechanics early (the day before race day was the busiest).

And number four: Have a little patience. “That’s really the hardest part of Ironman week – managing athletes’ timeline expectations,” Taylor Bushong, a traveling race mechanic working out of Bike Works Kona, told Sara Stover. “Managing the unrealistic ‘can you just’ requests. The understanding of the level of the request seems to be outside the scope of recognition.”

But while being a bike mechanic sounds like a thankless task, it has some upsides. The real kicker, featuring five carbon wheels and the town’s dump, is cleverly left until the final line.

Some charitable sporting endeavors fall flat while others just fly, and often there seems to be no logic as to which cause will capture the public mood.

Thankfully, for Ethan Hunger, the idea to complete a world-record number of super sprint triathlons within 24 hours to raise money for his local food bank in Bellingham, Washington, really took off.

If ever there was a classic case of nominative determinism, then this is it. Hunger v. Hunger actually started following the COVID pandemic, but as Travis Mundell found out, this year’s challenge was the most ambitious yet, helping push the initiative’s total fundraising beyond $1.2 million.

It’s life-affirming to see such dedication in action, not just from Hunger, but from the community that rolled out to support him, where putting all the proper procedures in place so the record could be ratified by Guinness reads as more grueling than all that swimming, biking, and running.

There’s probably not much more that needs adding to one of the most dramatic Ironman World Championship races in living memory. Having written a reaction piece on how the house (in this case, the Big Island) always wins versus the gambler, I’ve reflected more on how it just seems such a difficult race to get right. My first thought: If the pros can’t do it (see the DNF files here), what chance do the mere mortals have? Follow-up thought: Nobody racing here could ever be described as a mere mortal anyway.

#8818. How to Strengthen Your Arms and Wrists With Upward Plank Variations

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Upward Plank Pose variations first appeared in the June 2007 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

What direction do you face when you practice yoga? Probably whichever way your usual practice space dictates. But the old yogis were very clear that we should face either east or north when practicing, per the classical yoga text the Gheranda Samhita 5.48. Why?

Yoga scholar Alain Danielou writes that the four cardinal and four intermediate points of the compass have special significance. The thunderbolt-wielding Indra, lord of all the protectors and prototype of courage and power in Hindu mythology, guards the east.

By facing in a certain direction when we practice, we acknowledge and draw on energetic properties for support and inspiration. So again, why east and north? East is the quarter of the rising sun, which Hindus revere as the “breath of creatures” or the source of all earthly life.

The sun represents the embodied Self, its dawn the emergence of the “light” of spiritual self-awareness and insight. North is the quarter of the pole star, called dhruva (pronounced DREW-vah) in Sanskrit, meaning “fixed, eternal.” Its constancy amid the ever-wheeling night sky is considered the embodiment of willpower, certainly a quality all serious yogis covet. In India too, north is the realm of the majestic Himalayas, where Hindu tradition places the mythic mountain Meru, thought of as the “navel” of the earth as well as the bridge to the celestial world of the gods and goddesses.

What compass directions would you assign to the back and front of your body? According to the yogis, your back body is the west, your front body the east. In Sanskrit, paschima means both “back” and “west,” while purva means both “front” and “east.” So this terminology gives us the names of two common and related poses: Paschimottanasana (Intense Stretch of the West Pose or, more commonly, Seated Forward Bend), which stretches your back body, and Purvottanasana (Intense Stretch of the East or Upward Plank Pose)—pictured here—a slight backbend and front-body stretch that provides a nice counterpose to its western opposite.

Purvottanasana stretches you all the way from your ankles through the thighs, groins, and belly, up to the shoulders and throat. It also strengthens your wrists and the muscles on the backs of the upper arms (triceps) and firms the buttocks—which, if you believe popular media claims, is a primary benefit of yoga. It will also help improve your sense of balance and calm. And it’s a great counterpose to the commonly practiced Chaturanga Dandasana (Four-Limbed Staff Pose).

If you have serious wrist, shoulder, or neck problems, practice this pose only under the guidance of an experienced teacher. You’ll need a chair, a block, and a wall to practice some of these preparatory poses.

Sit on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you in Dandasana (Staff Pose). Rotate your thighs inward, big toes in, heels out, and press your palms to the floor slightly behind your buttocks with your fingers pointing forward toward your feet. If your shoulders protest, you can turn your fingers outward.

Bend your elbows and sink or hollow your front torso, spreading your scapulas as far away from your spine as possible. Rotate your upper arms inward and widen your elbows, letting the heads of your upper arm bones (humeri) jut forward. Enjoy the stretch between the scapulas for a minute or so.

Then straighten your elbows and lift your chest while leaving your lower body on the floor. Often, students simply squeeze their scapulas together and shove their lower front ribs forward, which hardens the front torso, restricting the free flow of breath, and compresses the low back. Instead, keep your scapulas wide and front torso soft.

Press the bases of your index fingers into the floor and hug your triceps against your humeri. As your elbows straighten out and your chest lifts, maintain the inward rotation of your upper arms, which will help the scapulas stay broad. Release your head back slightly, but don’t fully extend the neck. Trace the stretch along your front torso from your pubis to your sternum (breastbone).

Imagine directing your inhalations into the space behind your sternum (“imagine” because there’s no lung there, just your heart), increasing the lift of your chest. With each exhalation, reaffirm the opposing movements of the inner hands (down against the floor) and scapulas (up against your back). Hold for a minute or two. Repeat two or three times, until you feel confident you’ll be able to recreate the inward rotation of the thighs and arms and the actions of the hands and scapulas while maintaining the soft front torso when called on to do so in the more challenging circumstances of the full pose.

Next, sit on the front edge of a chair with your knees bent, heels directly below your knees. Wrap your hands around the back edge of the seat (for this first part of the exercise your upper arms will naturally rotate outward), thumbs pointing outward (Figure 1).

Inhale and slowly lift your buttocks away from the seat until your thighs, torso, and head form one long diagonal line, with your arms more or less perpendicular to the chair seat. Rotate your thighs slightly inward, and push (but don’t physically move) your knees away from your torso. The thigh rotation will tend to make your tailbone sag toward the floor, collapsing your belly, so firm your tailbone against your back pelvis and lengthen it. Hold this position for a minute, then sit back on the chair. On an inhalation, release the back edge of the seat and return to sitting upright. Take a few breaths.

If you like, repeat this exercise with your fingers turned forward, palms on the seat, and your upper arms rotated inward. Hold for one minute, release on an exhalation, and rest.

If you want to take this exercise to its limit, lift your buttocks again and extend your legs. Do your right leg first. Inhale and press out through your heel to straighten your knee, but suspend your foot a few inches off the floor. Then rotate your thigh inward, point your toes, and bring your sole to the floor. Just as the bases of your index forgers press the seat, so the base of your big toe presses on the floor. Repeat with the left leg. Once again, hold for a minute and release on an exhalation.

If you want to continue, brace the back legs of a chair against the wall and lay your block on the seat (if you’re using a wood block, cover the seat with a sticky mat to keep the block from sliding). Set the block on either its lowest or middle height near the front edge of the seat.

Sit on the floor right in front of the chair, knees bent, feet on the floor, heels 12 to 15 inches away from your buttocks, and lean back against the front edge of the seat. Press your hands on the floor with your fingers turned either forward, to the sides, or back—you choose—just in front of the feet of the chair legs.

Inhale and do what you did for the first part of the first exercise: Lift your thighs and torso parallel to the floor (heels below the knees), and then release your head back onto the block to take any pressure off your neck. If the block is too high or too low, come down and readjust. If you are having trouble opening your chest, it may help to reinforce the firmness of your palms against the floor, your scapulas against your back, and your triceps against the humeri. Then again, it may not.

Don’t get discouraged. Just practice this exercise every other day or so for the next few weeks, and you’ll be surprised how quickly things improve. Whatever happens, hold the pose for 30 seconds to a minute, then release to the floor on an exhalation. Smile.

If you can’t boost your chest, though, trying to extend your legs will probably make matters worse, so I don’t recommend it. But if your chest is reasonably lifted, then it’s acceptable to extend your legs.

Having trouble getting the balls of your feet, especially the bases of your big toes, on the floor? Position a rolled-up sticky mat on the floor where the balls of your feet will be when your legs are extended and press against that.

#8817. Is Cycling Good Cardio? Here's How It Compares to Running and Swimming

Learn how cycling compares to other cardio activities like walking, running, and swimming.

Riding a bike is as good a workout as it is a ton of fun. Hop on a bike—any kind—and your heart rate will pick up, your breathing rate will increase, and you’ll break a sweat. Whether you choose to fly over asphalt on a road bike, cruise back roads on a gravel setup, or push pedals in an indoor studio, you’re doing your mind and body big favors when you hop in the saddle.

One of the biggest payoffs? Cardio benefits. Read on for how cycling boosts your cardio fitness and how it stacks up to other forms of cardiovascular exercise, like running and using an elliptical.

Cardio exercise is any exercise that increases your heart rate and respiration (breathing rate). Cardio exercise can be aerobic or anaerobic. Broadly, what makes cardio aerobic or anaerobic is the intensity level of the exercise (and physiologically, the source of energy for that exercise).

Aerobic exercise, defined by the American College of Sports Medicine, is a rhythmic activity that uses large muscle groups and can be maintained continuously. This is also called steady-state exercise, and it can include running, walking, cycling, rowing, using the elliptical or stair-stepper, swimming, and hiking.

Anaerobic cardio exercise is high-intensity, and true anaerobic activity can only be performed for short periods of time; sprinting is a good example of anaerobic cardio exercise. Activities like jumping rope and mountain biking—and any of the aforementioned activities performed in high-intensity spurts—can also fit into this cardio category.

In any case, “cardio exercise often consists of extended periods of time with an elevated heart rate and an increase in oxygen demand,” says Alexander Rothstein, ACSM-certified exercise physiologist, strength and conditioning coach, and coordinator for the exercise science program at New York Institute of Technology.

“Performing cardio exercise will stress the cardiovascular system, which will signal the need for adaptation and cause improvements in the body’s ability to supply and utilize oxygen,” he explains.

The goal of cardio exercise is to increase the efficiency of your heart, lungs, and circulatory system, thereby improving your overall fitness and endurance.

“Cardiorespiratory fitness reflects the ability of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems to supply oxygen-rich blood to skeletal muscles during sustained physical activity,” says Joe Scarrella, triathlon coach and certified personal trainer at Life Time Chanhassen in Minnesota.

This type of fitness “is vitally important to health and wellness, especially to the ability of engaging in normal activities of daily living without excessive fatigue,” he says. “Because of its heart-strengthening and overall health benefits, cardio training should always be near the top of priorities when allocating time to a fitness program.”

Yes, cycling is cardio exercise—an excellent form of it, in fact. Cycling requires continuous movement that increases your heart rate. When you pedal, your heart works harder to pump blood to your muscles. This steady effort challenges your cardiovascular system, helping it become more efficient over time.

A cycling habit brings about a lot of benefits, including:

While cycling is a fantastic form of cardio, it’s not your only option. Here’s a look at how it measures up to other popular forms of cardio exercise.

Cycling burns more calories per hour than walking, according to the Compendium of Physical Activity. Cycling at a leisurely pace (less than 10 mph) can burn about 330 calories per hour for a 180-pound person. Walking at a leisurely pace (2.5 mph) burns about 246 calories per hour for a person of the same weight.

Both cycling and walking are low-impact exercises, making them ideal for those with joint pain or arthritis. Cycling allows more room for increasing speed or resistance without changing joint impact, which offers a more intense cardio workout for individuals with joint concerns.

On the flip side, walking is a weight-bearing form of exercise, while cycling is not, so walking could be the better choice for individuals with bone density concerns.

Walking is more accessible because it requires no equipment beyond a good pair of shoes. Cycling, on the other hand, requires much more gear: a bike and helmet, at minimum, plus safe space to ride outdoors. An indoor stationary bike or bike trainer is required for cycling inside, and while there are budget options, it’s still an investment.

If you're looking for a simple, accessible form of low-intensity cardio, walking might be the best option. However, for a more intense workout that’s still easy on the joints, cycling is the way to go.

Running tends to burn more calories than cycling, because it’s more difficult for many individuals to achieve the increase in heart rate that they may get from running, Rothstein says. It may take longer to burn as many calories as one would while running.

According to data from the Compendium of Physical Activity, cycling at a “self-selected moderate pace” burns about 573 calories in one hour for a 180-pound person. That same person may burn about 615 calories “jogging at a self-selected pace,” according to the Compendium.

Running is a high-impact exercise, which can place stress on your joints, especially your knees and ankles. Cycling, in contrast, is low-impact, making it a better option for people with joint issues or those recovering from injuries.

Both running and cycling primarily work your lower body, including your quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves. During cycling, your core and back muscles may be recruited more to maintain posture on the bike, depending on the style of your bike. When running, your core, back, and arms all work to maintain posture and stability.

If joint health is a concern or you prefer a lower-impact workout, cycling is the better choice. Running is a viable option for people who can handle the joint impact and/or don’t have the means to invest in a bike or stationary bike.

Swimming and cycling burn similar amounts of calories, depending on intensity. According to the Compendium of Physical Activity, swimming freestyle at a vigorous pace for one hour burns about 800 calories for a 180-pound person. The same person would burn about 818 calories cycling at 14 to 16 mph, which may be a moderate or vigorous effort depending on your fitness level.

Swimming has virtually no impact on joints because the water supports your body, making it an ideal option for those with joint pain, injuries, or mobility issues.

Cycling is also low-impact but not quite as easy on the body as swimming. Depending on the type of bike, some individuals may struggle with mobility when cycling. (For example, on a road bike with drop bars, it can strain the neck and back to reach them. In such a case, a bike with an upright frame might be a better choice.)

Swimming is a full-body workout, engaging both your upper and lower body, as well as your core. You’ll recruit more muscles in the arms and shoulders while swimming, compared to cycling, which primarily targets the lower body.

If you want a no-impact, full-body workout, swimming might be your best option. Keep in mind that sticking to a swimming plan requires having access to a lap pool, which isn’t feasible for everyone. Even though a bike can be a big investment, it may be the more accessible option in this case.

Cycling burns more calories than elliptical training at the same effort level. For a 180-pound person, cycling at a moderate pace (12 to 14 mph) burns around 654 calories in 60 minutes, while a moderate 60-minute session on the elliptical burns about 409 calories.

Both are low-impact exercises, making them suitable for people with joint concerns. The elliptical may provide an advantage for people who struggle with mobility, because you remain in an upright position and don’t have to significantly flex the spine like on the bike.

Elliptical machines engage both the upper and lower body, while cycling primarily focuses on your lower body, though the upper body and core are still engaged to some extent while riding a bike.

If you prefer a workout that engages your whole body, the elliptical may be the better choice. However, if you like the idea of getting outside and/or exercising with a community, cycling offers a more dynamic experience in that sense.

Overall, “all forms of cardio are similar in their cardiovascular health and weight loss benefits,” says Rothstein. “The increased oxygen demand and overall cardiovascular stress will result in improved health and well-being. The ability to burn calories is also similar even if the rate might be different between types of cardio.”

Adaptations in stamina are where the most significant differences lie, says Rothstein. “We adapt based on the specific training stimulus, so in cyclists, stamina improvements will mostly be shown in cycling performance. For example, if you train cycling, you will not improve your running unless you also train as a runner. This is because even though both have cardiovascular adaptation benefits, the muscular adaptations will be specific to the type of training.”

In other words: Train what you want to be good at doing.

#8815. Choosing a Gravel Bike? These 12 Editor-Tested Models Deliver the Tire Clearance, Geometry, and Value That Matter

From bikepacking to gravel racing, these tested bikes cover every kind of dirt-road ride.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Instead of riding busy, congested city and suburban roads, many cyclists now head to lightly traveled gravel and unimproved roads. Gravel riding is a great way to see beautiful fall foliage, enjoy the fresh air, and avoid traffic. Most brands sell at least one gravel model; some offer multiple gravel platforms or bikes designed for particular gravel-riding niches. Whether you need a new bicycle for a big gravel fondo or race, a versatile bike for multi-surface rides, or a rig for bikepacking adventures, there’s a gravel bike for you.

The term “gravel riding” is very broad and doesn’t necessarily mean riding on gravel surfaces the entire ride. Gravel rides can include anything from hard-packed dirt roads (which you can often ride on a traditional road bike) to singletrack trails (typically associated with mountain bikes). Gravel riding also includes almost any other type of unimproved roadway; forest access roads, farm roads, jeep roads, rail trails, and canal paths are all commonly lumped under the gravel umbrella. And many of the best gravel routes and events incorporate a few of these surfaces.

Because they get ridden in such varied terrain, gravel bikes come in many shapes and sizes. They span the gamut of aero-optimized bikes that look similar to WorldTour road bikes to full suspension models that resemble mountain bikes with dropbars—But most gravel bikes fall somewhere in between these polar extremes. Most gravel bikes share a few key traits: Generous tire clearance, a more upright riding position, and geometry that prioritizes stability and confidence on rough surfaces.

Buying Tip: Don’t pass on a great gravel bike because you don’t like its tires. Focus on a bike’s tire clearance rather than the stock rubber’s tread or width. Brands usually equip gravel bikes with tires that work well in average conditions. If those tires don’t work for you, it’s a simple fix. Upgrading to tires that better suit your needs is often the best—and easiest—first change you can make, and it usually shaves weight.

The Canyon Grizl is a great all-arounder. It’s a gravel bike built for all sorts of adventures, whether it’s a casual after-work gravel spin, commuting around town, or a multi-day bikepacking trip. The SRAM Apex XPLR 1x12 drivetrain shifts quickly and has a wide gear range. The Grizl’s carbon frame also helps dampen the bumps on rougher roads and trails.

Since we tested the bike a few seasons ago, platform updates have improved its capability and appeal. The Grizl now features clearance for wider tires (up to 56mm), internal downtube storage, and an easily sourced UDH hanger. If this model doesn't speak to you, Canyon offers several Grizl options priced from $1,899 to $4,699.

If you don’t have thousands of dollars to spend but need a bike for riding actual gravel roads, your choices might seem limited. However, if you dig into brands’ websites and look for budget picks, you will find a few gems. The $1,300 Salsa Journeyer Essa is a good example; it stands out for its robust parts, wide tires, and size range.

Unlike some cheaper gravel bikes you may find on Amazon, the Journeyer’s aluminum frame comes in six sizes to fit riders from 4’8” to 6’5”. Additionally, it’s available through REI. This way, you’ll have warranty support if anything goes awry, and the bike is professionally assembled (if you choose in-store pickup).

For components, Salsa equips this Journeyer model with Shimano’s 1x8-speed Essa group (including Shimano mechanical disc brakes)—the parts aren’t fancy, but they’re robust. The only negative point of the Journeyer Essa is its standard QR dropouts, which make upgrading to lighter-weight or tubeless wheels slightly more difficult.

The Topstone 1 is Cannondale’s top-tier aluminum gravel bike. Designed for versatility and adventure, it’s equally at home on pavement or dirt, with a utilitarian setup that includes mounts for racks, bags, fenders, and extra bottles—perfect for long-haul rides. But don’t mistake utilitarian for boring; the Topstone still feels lively and efficient on the road, making it a great choice for days when your rides lean more toward pavement.

This model comes with 37mm tires, but the frame clears up to 45mm rubber. This allows you to choose tires for the terrain and rides you take. The Shimano GRX 2x11 drivetrain is another standout, offering a wide gear range for steep, rough climbs while keeping gear jumps tight—something you’ll appreciate when riding extended stretches of pavement.

Salsa practically invented the modern gravel bike with its Warbird, and the Minnesota-based brand remains as relevant as ever. Its recently launched Flyway C is a lightweight and responsive gravel bike for gravel racing or all-day rides. It features generous tire clearance (up to 57mm), a UDH dropout (for easy replacement or upgrades), and revised geometry (long reach and short stem) for improved control on rough terrain.

Several Flyway configurations are available (I tested the Force AXS XPLR model), and I think the Apex Eagle AXS model sits right in the sweet spot for many riders. As the name suggests, Salsa outfits this bike with a combination of SRAM’s Apex AXS and Eagle X1 AXS 1x electronic drivetrains to provide a superwide gear range. In addition to the great components, Salsa also equips this model with a flared carbon bar and a carbon seatpost. It’s an all-around great package for anyone looking to up their gravel game this season.

Trek’s Checkpoint ALR 5 is versatile, well-rounded, and a great pick for riders new to gravel cycling. In his review, Chabanov says, “The value sweet spot: modern geometry and feature set borrowed from the [Checkpoint] SL, delivered in a durable alloy package with smart mounts and standards—at a starting price that leaves room in the budget for meaningful upgrades. Because there are no proprietary parts, upgrading and swapping things like the handlebar, stem, and seatpost is super easy.”

Overall, the Checkpoint ALR gets far more right than it gets wrong. Sure, you can nitpick the stock wheels and tires—or wish for the carbon model’s downtube storage and IsoSpeed—but those trade-offs help keep the price in check while preserving what matters. This bike has confident handling, generous tire room, real-world durability, and an upgrade-friendly platform. The result is a thoroughly well-thought-out aluminum gravel bike that feels ready for anything from weeknight dirt spins to loaded weekend overnighters, or even that gravel race that’s on your bucket list.

If you’re a gravel racer on a budget, or simply like going fast and don’t have the money for bikes like the Specialized S-Works Crux or Colnago G5-X, Canyon’s new Grail should be on your short list. As my colleague Matt Phillips described in his review of the revised platform, “And “fast” was the word that stuck with me as I rode the Grail across singletrack, dirt roads, and paved roads. It feels fast. It made me feel like I was fast.”

Wide tire clearance is one of the latest Grail’s upgrade highlights. At 57mm, the frame and fork can fit the widest gravel tires and even 29 x 2.25-inch mountain bike rubber for rocky terrain or singletrack (or if you want a super comfortable feel). The entry-tier Grail CF SL models use a heavier carbon frame than the Grail CFR and CF SLX versions, but only 140 grams more than the high-end CFR bike (about the weight of a standard butyl inner tube). All models feature a carbon cockpit, seatpost, and wheels.

The Grail CF 7 Speed is a great bang-for-the-buck gravel racer. Canyon equips it with SRAM’s excellent Rival XPLR AXS 1x13 electronic shifting gravel groupset. Although Canyon doesn’t ship this model with a power meter, you can easily upgrade to a Rival power crank for under $200.

You’re not buying this bike for its tire clearance, gear-hauling options, or aerodynamics; plenty of other gravel bikes do those things better than the G5-X. You buy this bike because it’s a Colnago.

On fast gravel roads, double track, and even technical singletrack, Colnago’s superb geometry, fit, and ride comfort won me over. The G5-X feels super composed and planted when descending and over choppy gravel road sections. The bike is precise and refined—pick your line and take it. On climbs and rolling terrain, the G5-X is comfortable and efficient, and responds immediately to bursts of power.

Overall, Colnago’s latest bike is a beautifully fast gravel racer with sublime handling. However, while the G5-X has more tire clearance (53mm) than the brand’s previous gravel offerings, it falls a few millimeters shy of the clearance found on some new gravel models. This will matter to some, but many riders will seek out the G5-X for the name on the downtube and Colnago’s cycling legacy.

Inspired by the Tour Divide—America’s longest mountain bike race—this bike carries more and handles a wider range of terrain than almost any other gravel bike. It’s loaded with mounts for racks, camping gear, bike accessories, and water bottles.

Although it’s intended for burly rides, the Cutthroat features a carbon frame and fork, which helps to reduce weight. And Salsa’s Class 5 Vibration Reduction System absorbs uneven terrain for a more comfortable ride. The Cutthroat C GRX model also includes a Shimano GRX 1x12 mechanical, wide-range drivetrain and a dropper seatpost.

With its steel frame, bar-end shifters, and triple-chainring crankset, the Masi Giramondo is a throwback to a bygone era of bicycle design and construction. While the bike’s aesthetic and features might not appeal to athletes chasing fast finishing times in 200-mile gravel races, it’s perfect for riders who want to hit the gravel, dirt, or paved roads loaded down with gear for touring adventures.

Unlike most bikes sold for touring or bikepacking, the Giramondo comes stock with a front and rear rack. This means you won’t have to add them to your bike-buying budget. To make it slightly easier to pedal your fully laden bike up hills, Masi equips this model with a triple crankset. While triples aren’t as trendy as 1x drivetrains, they offer an extremely wide gear range: Its lowest gear is close to many mountain bikes, and the highest gear rivals many gravel race bikes.

While State labels this model “All-Road,” it’s very much a modern gravel bike. Starting at $2,400 for a complete bike, or $1,400 for the frameset, the All-Road Carbon checks all of the boxes without totally draining your bank account. It accommodates up to 2.2-inch tires (complete builds ship with 50mm Vittoria T50s), is UDH-compatible, and takes a T47 bottom bracket. The All-Road Carbon also features internal storage in the frame’s downtube with a Fidlock magnetic latch.

The Carbon All-Road’s frame isn’t super aero-shaped, and it doesn’t use funky proprietary parts—and that’s a good thing. This bike is made for riders who prioritize durability and functionality over flashy graphics, pro teams, and marketing hype. The All-Road’s geometry falls on the “race-inspired” end of the spectrum, compared with the more upright feel of adventure-style gravel bikes. The bike carries speed on hardpack dirt and gravel and feels adequately stiff when sprinting and out of corners. The ride quality is a little harsher than premium gravel offerings, but a complete Carbon All-Road costs less than most big-name brands’ frames.

The all-new Specialized Crux has shed its cyclocross roots and turned into a modern gravel racer. In his review of the fifth-generation platform, Test Editor Dan Chabanov says, “It is built around the demands of professional gravel racers, and around the idea that going fast off-road now means balancing low weight, aero efficiency, tire clearance, and stability rather than just chasing the lightest possible frame.” The result is an excellent gravel bike that, while optimized for racers, anyone who loves going fast can enjoy.

Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips rode the Crux 5 for several days on the gravel roads in Durango, Colorado, and walked away very impressed by the updated bike. “The Crux 5 leans more toward stability and predictability,” he said. “It’s fast, yes. Very fast. But it’s also composed. It lets you settle in. It doesn’t feel like it’s trying to prove something every second.”

That balance is a big part of what makes the Crux great for non-racers. “A lot of us don’t need a gravel bike that only makes sense at 300 watts,” Phillips said. “We need a bike that feels sharp when you want to go hard, but isn’t a pain in the ass the rest of the time.”

Of the five models in the Crux 5 lineup, the Crux 5 Comp stands out for its performance-to-price ratio. It features a slightly heavier carbon frame than the high-end S-Works variants, but it has the same great geometry, tire clearance, and aerodynamics. Specialized equips the Comp model with SRAM’s excellent Rival AXS XPLR 1x brakes and drivetrain, and the bike rolls on 26mm-wide inner diameter alloy wheels wrapped in 45mm-wide Pathfinder tubeless tires.

The bike used by two-time gravel World Champion Marianne Vos (🐐), the Áspero-5 is what happens when Cervélo combines aerodynamic principles of the Paris-Roubaix-winning S5 with a gravel race bike. This bike is eye-wateringly fast on smoother gravel and dirt roads. The Áspero-5 is fast enough that many riders will want to use it on paved roads too.

Much of this speed advantage comes from Cervélo’s aerodynamic tuning of the frame, fork, and bar; the 42mm-wide Vittoria Corsa Pro Control TLR rubber enhances it. An excellent road tire for broken pavement in narrow sizes, the Pro Control really shines in the 700x42c size on dirt and gravel surfaces.

With so many types and sub-niches of gravel bikes, it can seem overwhelming to pick the right one. My first advice: start by honestly evaluating the terrain you ride, then consider how you like to ride it. From there, narrow your choices to the bikes that meet your budget, personal tastes, and other factors.

Racing-oriented bikes typically feature an aggressive fit and handling with fewer mounts for bags or extra water bottles. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes built for long-distance, multi-day adventures, equipped with all the mounts you could want for gear and accessories. In between, there’s a wide range of subtle variations that can make a big difference.

12-week plan for 50- to 75-mile gravel races

8-week plan to take your cycling to the next level

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8814. These Are the World’s Fastest Marathoners

Here’s a complete list of the world record-holders and all-time top 26.2-mile runners.

Below you’ll find tables detailing several marathon superlatives:

Note that we said “on record-eligible courses.” That’s why Eliud Kipchoge’s 1:59:40 in Vienna isn’t on the list from 2019. That time doesn’t count for record purposes because standard competition rules for pacing and fluids weren’t followed. Similarly, times from the Boston course can’t be on the list, because of its point-to-point layout and too-great net elevation drop.

Each marathoner appears on the first list, for the fastest performers in history, only once. The third set of tables, for fastest performances in history, allows for a runner to appear more than once. For example, Kelvin Kiptum and Eliud Kipchoge both appear twice in the fastest-performances list for men.

All tables are current as of November 1, 2026.

Picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

Two other paths exist if you're working with different currencies:

One critical nuance: HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, not credit card spend. Hawaiian does have a co-branded credit card, but it's not a top earner for most people's daily spend. This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

Another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

Finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. Many programs — particularly those involving European carriers — tack on $300–$600 in surcharges that gut your redemption's net value. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Go to hawaiianairlines.com and use the 'Book' tool, selecting 'Reward Travel' as your travel type. Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. You're looking for economy award space priced at 7,500 miles. Availability on interisland routes is almost always wide open — this is one of the best availability scores (5/5) of any sweet spot in this guide series, but it costs nothing to confirm before you transfer.

If you don't have a HawaiianMiles account, create one at hawaiianairlines.com — it takes about two minutes and is free. Note your HawaiianMiles number. You'll need it for the transfer step.

From Amex Membership Rewards: Log into your Amex account, navigate to 'Membership Rewards,' select 'Transfer Points,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines HawaiianMiles as the destination. Enter your HawaiianMiles number and the number of miles you want to transfer (at minimum, 7,500 per person you're booking). Transfers process in 1–2 days.

From Bilt Rewards: Log into your Bilt app or biltrewards.com, navigate to 'Redeem,' select 'Transfer to Airline Partner,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines at 1:1. Same 1–2 day transfer window.

From Marriott Bonvoy: Use this only as a last resort due to the 3:1 ratio. Navigate to Bonvoy's transfer portal and select HawaiianMiles. Allow up to 5 days.

Once your miles land (check your HawaiianMiles account balance), return to hawaiianairlines.com, log in, and re-run your award search. Select the flight you want, confirm the 7,500-mile price, and proceed through checkout. Taxes on interisland awards are typically just a few dollars — no fuel surcharges apply.

HawaiianMiles opens its booking window 330 days out. If you're planning a Hawaii trip far in advance and have specific flight times in mind, you can search and book early. That said, given the excellent availability on these routes, booking 2–4 weeks out is usually fine.

This is rare for interisland routes, but if it happens, try: searching adjacent dates, looking at different departure times on the same route, or checking alternate routing (e.g., OGG to LIH instead of HNL to LIH directly). Interisland availability doesn't fluctuate the way transatlantic business class does.

Let's make this concrete. You're planning a two-week Hawaii trip for two people. You've booked your Honolulu arrival flight separately, and now you need to connect the dots between islands: Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) mid-trip, and then Maui (OGG) to Lihue, Kauai (LIH) before heading home.

The cash price check: Pull up hawaiianairlines.com and look at what these tickets retail for. On a typical mid-trip travel day, the HNL→OGG segment is priced at $189 per person. The OGG→LIH hop runs $149 per person. For two travelers, that's $676 in cash — before you've bought a single plate of shave ice.

The points price: Each segment costs 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person in economy. Two passengers, two flights: 30,000 HawaiianMiles total, plus roughly $10–$20 in taxes and fees across both bookings. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP calculation: You're replacing $676 in cash spending with 30,000 miles. That's 2.25 cents per point — well above the 0.8–1.2 cpp you'd expect on typical HawaiianMiles redemptions, and solidly within the 1.3–3.3 cpp sweet spot range for this redemption.

What the experience looks like: Hawaiian's interisland product is no-frills — these are 20-to-40-minute flights on Boeing 717s. You won't get a meal or premium service. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

For the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. You budgeted for interisland flights; now that budget goes to a sunset sailing charter or a snorkeling excursion instead. The points paid for the planes. The cash funds the memories.

Do: Transfer Points in the Right Batch Size HawaiianMiles doesn't allow you to transfer partial miles back out, so calculate exactly how many you need before initiating a transfer. For two passengers on two flights, that's 30,000 miles. Transfer exactly that amount — or a small buffer — rather than dumping your entire MR balance into a program you may not use frequently.

Do: Use Amex MR or Bilt as Your Primary Earning Strategy Since HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, your accumulation plan should center on transferable currencies. The Amex Gold Card (4x on dining and groceries) and Amex Platinum (5x on flights) are elite MR earners. Bilt's no-annual-fee card earning on rent is underused by the ChooseFI community for exactly this kind of transfer.

Do: Search for Availability Before You Transfer This is worth repeating as a pro tip because new points travelers make this mistake constantly. Transfer speeds are 1–2 days for Amex MR and Bilt. Don't transfer points and then discover the flight you wanted is sold out. Always confirm availability first, then transfer, then book immediately once miles land.

Avoid: Using Marriott Bonvoy for This Transfer At a 3:1 ratio, you'd spend 22,500 Bonvoy points for a 7,500-mile award. Bonvoy points are worth approximately 0.7–0.9 cpp on their own best redemptions. The math doesn't hold here — save your Bonvoy points for hotel redemptions.

Do: Consider the Merger Context Hawaiian Airlines is in the process of merging with Alaska Airlines, and HawaiianMiles may eventually transition into Alaska Mileage Plan. Pay attention to program announcements. This could change transfer partners, award pricing, or program structure. The current sweet spot exists now — book it while the program operates under its current rules.

Avoid: Waiting for a 'Better' Redemption on These Miles HawaiianMiles are a limited-use currency. They're excellent for interisland and mainland-to-Hawaii flights, but they don't transfer to other airlines and don't unlock international business class sweet spots. If you've got miles in this program, use them for exactly what they're designed for — Hawaiian flights — rather than letting them sit hoping for a better opportunity that may never come.

Do: Book Multiple Segments in a Single Trip If you're doing a true multi-island itinerary, every interisland hop is 7,500 miles. Three islands means two hops — 15,000 miles per person. Plan your island sequence to minimize backtracking, and book all segments at once once your miles transfer.
